#861. Kane’s Ballon d’Or triumph a glorious riposte to celebrity fawning of ceremony | Barney Ronay

The England captain spoke movingly on a night of deserving winners and unintentional hilarity in London

Well, there’s something new. Football: now available in new, genuinely heartwarming flavour.

There was a lovely moment at London’s Palladium theatre on Monday, with the clock creeping towards 11pm at the end of a startlingly shrill and bloated evening of never‑ending awards and never-ending award‑related excitement.

Not just for Harry Kane, who is now the 2026 men’s Ballon d’Or winner, and in the process placed indelibly in that lineage of elite footballers. But also, frankly, for anyone watching, as Kane stood on stage gazing a little shyly at his golden orb, and kicked off his speech by thanking everyone, paying tribute to everyone, everywhere, then finally cracking into tears and a strangled croak as he thanked his parents for sacrifices made, his wife for always being there, and even, in slightly jarring vibe-shift from the warm honeyed tone, José Mourinho.

Even Kane’s biggest advocates will rarely claim their man is one of a kind, sui generis, in the mode of the Ronaldo-Messi godhead. But Kane is exactly this in his own admirably humble way.

Not just an exceptional footballer, the best, most deserving men’s player in the world this year, a European golden boot, scorer of 89 goals since August 2025, Bundesliga champion, World Cup semi-final captain, model of extreme professionalism and care. He’s also quite clearly the nicest man, if not just in football, then possibly the world.

Or at least it felt like that as he walked off in that very dear and tender way, the centre of the world in that moment, but also just keen to get off the stage and let everyone get on with clearing up.

It would be wrong to say Kane’s victory in the final vote of the night redeemed the grotesqueness of the ceremonies itself. There was a roomful of hugely deserving winners here. But Kane hits particularly hard.

And the Ballon d’Or is, let us be clear, a horrendous event, albeit a supremely popular horrendous event. There was the usual pomp around the ceremony, staged this year at a fancy theatre close to Oxford Circus.

This isn’t sport. It’s celebrity culture, red‑carpet fawning, the worship of images and people, and fame. Football isn’t supposed to be cocooned this way, to send the message that there are barriers and ropes and special people. Yeah, well, good luck with that.

The night kicked off with French Montana in spotless white tuxedo performing on an open-air double-decker bus. He definitely speaks, clearly, carried well, seemed enthusiastic. If it all goes south from here, the evidence suggests French Montana could, at the very least, get a job as a London tour bus operator.

Before long Thierry Henry and Kate Scott glided on stage, half an hour late, to add a little deft and easy charm to a furious schedule of pots and prizes.

And the awards came thick and fast. The Spain manager, Luis de la Fuente, was named coach of the year. “I hope in the future I will become in English better,” were his first words at the lectern, throwing his hat in the ring for a disastrous pension-padding six months at Manchester United two years from now.

There was a lovely moment as Burna Boy came on to present the Socrates award for charitable works to Bukayo Saka. He was asked if there were footballers who had inspired his love for the game. At which point he looked at Thierry and said, “definitely, one of them’s standing right there”, and of course he said it in his Burna Boy voice, looking Thierry deep in the eyes so smooth and deep, just almost an impossibly sexy moment.

The Ballon d’Or can be unintentionally hilarious at times such as these. There were just so, so many video tributes, so much excitingly portentous music. This is a stage where everyone happening at every moment is very clearly the most important thing ever to happen, superseded only by the next thing to happen on that stage, and then the thing after that.

The degree of fawning is startling at first, but glazed by familiarity before long. At one point Cristiano Ronaldo appeared very briefly in a fact-cut big-screen montage and the crowd shrieked a song, clutched its hand to its fevered throat, collapsed into the aisles in sheer priapic excitement.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Although by the time the original Ronaldo emerged onstage at 10.44pm, there was a sense of the genuinely vertiginous company Kane was about to join. Ronaldo read out the name inside the envelope, and the hall collapsed into cheers and yells and roars as Kane appeared onstage.

And yes the Ballon d’Or is a fundamentally silly thing on its own terms. It jars with the basic concept of team sport, promoting instead the opposite of sport, the opposite of team culture, the modern disease of fawning parasocial engagement with star names. In many ways the world would be a better place if the Ballon d’Or was simply abolished, as an example to all who pore over reels and clips and the imagined qualities of their celebrity paramours.

But it is also fascinating, unignorable, and endlessly moreish. All the more so this time. Kane as the Ballon d’Or 2026 is a genuinely fine, uplifting, instructive moment in the spotlight.

It is always tempting to talk about the journey these players make. Everyone has a backstory. Most footballers come from adversity. Kane has this, in his own way, 16 years into a professional career which has names such as Leyton Orient, Millwall, Leicester and Norwich on the timelines. He was unexceptional as a junior, didn’t stand out as particularly skilful or big or outstanding in his numbers. He played as a holding midfielder for a bit while Spurs decided what to do with him.

Kane worked relentlessly. He was Millwall young player of the year in 2012, fitting bookend to the Ballon. He made it because he simply refused to go away, to stop working, honed instead the deeper skills in his quiver, the purity of his shooting, the range of his passing long and short.

And Kane is exceptional in other ways. Without ever peacocking around promoting his brand, without really trying he remains the most likable, authentic, role‑model‑ish modern-day England player. For a man who never talks big or acts big he has a happy knack of becoming the key player wherever he goes. Perhaps Kane has become cool now. He has always been likable, with that mild-mannered air of a kindly Victorian chimney sweep with a hamster in his waistcoat watch pocket. In the Bayern years, Kane has become leaner, more glossed and handsome, jawline, tan, iconic Vampire hairline.

Mainly he expresses a common confusion about what talent really is. Talent isn’t simply moments. Talent is also application, focus, craft, the ability to work, to make others better.

And yet his elite career has also been oddly grudging. Somehow the idea has always been out there that Kane is undeserving of these accolades, despite his own mildness and humility, his obvious team qualities, his relentless delivery of goals, effort, leadership. It is a genuinely odd conclusion given the opposite is so manifestly true, that this is an entirely uplifting story of overachievement, of hard work and applied intelligence, as opposed to the kind of talent that just needs to be flame‑throwered in the right direction.

It is undeniably true that Kane’s levels can drop dramatically when he can’t perform at his full physical capacity. There have been moments where it has been tempting to wonder if he’s gone far enough as England’s captain in the past few years, if his body and his talent deserve a little care.

Well, that just shows how wrong you can be.

#860. Germany's Merz says erosion of global order means middle powers in Europe and Asia must be more assertive

During a visit to Singapore, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Europe and Germany want to increase free trade with open competition, reliability and a rules-based order.

This blog is now closed. Below is a roundup of the top stories in Germany on Tuesday, October 27, 2026:

Don't want to miss our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google.

Thank you for joining our coverage of German news on Tuesday.

We look forward to bringing you the latest again on Wednesday in a fresh blog.

On the first day of his farewell tour in China, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier urged the German business community to act with confidence in the Chinese market.

"When you travel in China, you're amazed at how highly Germany and German technology are still valued here," he said in Hefei. "That's why we can act with confidence in these markets."

Steinmeier did not bring any companies with him to China as part of his delegation, as his final trip was intended to focus on culture and science.

Nevertheless, the first day of the trip in Hefei, the capital of Anhui Province, revolved primarily around the economy. Steinmeier visited the Volkswagen China Technology Company (VCTC). About three years ago, Europe's largest automaker opened a research center for electric mobility there, which today employs 3,000 people.

Johannes Volkmann, a lawmaker accompanying Steinmeier in China, warned that the German economy must not "lose its leadership in innovation."

"I'm taking this call to action with me from here to do more to improve competitive conditions at home," he said, adding that Germany must avoid creating new dependencies "by allowing innovation and value creation to take place only outside Europe."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Steinmeier called for Europe to reposition itself and reorganize its economic instruments with its growing trade deficit with China in mind.

"The trade surplus that China is accumulating naturally causes us concern because the successful model of economic cooperation is becoming unbalanced," he said. "We must strive to ensure that economic cooperation does not come to an end, but that it continues — to the mutual benefit of both sides."

Germany's trade deficit with China amounted to just under €90 billion ($100 billion) in 2025. According to the Federal Statistical Office, China exported goods worth €170.6 billion to Germany, and German exports to China amounted to €81.3 billion.

Across the 27-member EU, the deficit amounted to almost €197 billion in the first half of 2026, according to EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic.

Additional reporting by Rosalia Romaniec in Hefei.

A German court denied a defense request to end the trial of a former Ukrainian army officer who stands accused of sabotaging the Nord Stream gas pipelines.

Serhii Kuznietsov, 50, went on trial this month at the Hamburg state court, charged with causing an explosion, damaging property, disrupting public services and being an "accomplice to war crimes" by attacking civilian infrastructure.

Prosecutors accuse him of being the ringleader of the destruction, considered one of Europe's biggest acts of post-World War II sabotage. He is alleged to have carried out the explosions together with six others.

His lawyers said the charges should be dismissed, arguing that, as a former soldier, Kuznietsov was obligated by Ukrainian law not to speak for national security reasons and could face severe penalties in Ukraine if he did. They argued that, under German law, anyone who cannot speak on his or her own behalf cannot be convicted.

The Hamburg court ruled Kuznietsov's defense was not limited under German law and that freedom to testify is not limited by a foreign country's conditions of service.

The undersea explosions on September 26, 2022, damaged the Nord Stream 1 pipeline, which brought Russian natural gas to Germany until Moscow cut off supplies in August 2022.

The blasts also damaged the Nord Stream 2 pipeline, which never went into service. Germany suspended the pipeline's certification process shortly before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Italian authorities detained Kuznietsov last year. He was publicly named in extradition proceedings that led to his transfer to Germany in November.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has denied allegations that his country was involved in the pipeline blasts.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

German carmaker Mercedes-Benz has cut its forecast for 2026, with difficult market conditions in China and higher fourth-quarter cost expectations set to negatively impact profits, the company said on Tuesday.

Markets were quick to take note of the announcement, and Mercedes shares dropped 3.4% in trading on Tuesday morning.

The move makes Mercedes the third big German carmaker to lower its outlook for 2026 after BMW and VW took similar steps.

Mercedes-Benz CEO Ola Kaellenius has called on German employees to work more without pay while also expanding manufacturing operations in Hungary, where he said costs are about 70% lower than in Germany.

Mercedes currently expects an adjusted car profit margin of 2% to 3% in 2026, compared to the 3% to 5% in the previous guidance.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Like many German automakers, Mercedes has faced weak sales in China. German carmakers have struggled in the world's largest car market with sluggish demand and increased competition from local manufacturers.

Mercedes vehicle deliveries in China — last year already at their lowest level since 2016 — fell a further 29% in the nine months to the end of September.

Mercedes also released third-quarter figures earlier than planned, which showed that the company generated just €172 million ($191 million) in free cash flow from its vehicle business, down on the €422 million forecast by financial market experts.

Before interest and tax, Mercedes posted an operating profit of €1.77 billion — more than double the €750 million recorded a year earlier, according to the preliminary figures. But last year's stats were significantly impacted by one-time expenses, especially related to job cuts and legal disputes.

Adjusted for one-off items, the operating profit margin in the passenger car business stood at 2.5%, down on the 4.8% recorded a year earlier.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The German agency responsible for finding a final repository for nuclear waste (BGE) has eliminated five states from its search.

Berlin, Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate, Saxony and Saarland were deemed unsuitable for long-term radioactive waste storage.

In a report issued Tuesday, the BGE said it had limited its search to 5% of Germany, down from 25% in 2025. The federal agency aims to suggest suitable locations for final evaluation by the end of 2027.

Regions in northern, northwestern, southern and eastern Germany remain under consideration as locations for final storage facilities.

Germany's nuclear waste is currently stored in 16 above-ground interim storage facilities.

The BGE assessments evaluate regions' geological conditions and their ability to safely contain highly radioactive material. Granite, salt, and clay are generally considered potentially suitable types of rock and areas with damaged or compromised subsurface conditions, places with mines or volcanos have been active, are not eligible as final disposal sites.

Germany needs to find a repository for approximately 27,000 cubic meters of highly radioactive nuclear waste generated over more than 60 years of nuclear power generation. The site is expected to ensure safety for 1 million years. The last German nuclear power plants were decommissioned in April 2023.

BGE said its goal remains finding the site that offers the highest level of safety for highly radioactive waste.

The agency's recommendations, however, are not legally binding and it will be up to German lawmakers to determine the final disposal site.

Convicted right-wing terrorist Beate Zschäpe's request for early release from prison was denied with a court ruling that she would remain behind bars for at least nine more years.

Munich's Higher Regional Court on Tuesday set her minimum term at at least 24 years and refused to suspend the sentence to probation. By determining her guilt to be particularly severe, the court effectively ruled out her release after 15 years, which, including her time in pretrial detention, would have expired this year.

The Munich court said Zschäpe, currently 51, still had a good chance of leaving prison alive.

The decision is not yet legally binding, and the defense and the Federal Prosecutor's Office can appeal.

Zschäpe had been sentenced to life in prison in 2018 as an accomplice in the National Socialist Underground (NSU) murders that killed 10 people, mainly individuals with an immigrant background as well as a police officer.

The terror group went undetected for a decade. Zschäpe's fellow NSU members, Uwe Mundlos and Uwe Böhnhardt, injured several people with bomb attacks in Cologne and killed themselves to avoid arrest in 2011.

Under normal conditions, a convict who receives a life sentence in Germany can apply for parole after 15 years.

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius, along with his counterparts from France, Italy, Poland and the UK, authored an op-ed calling Russia "the most acute and long-term threat to Euro-Atlantic security and stability."

In the article, published online and in Tuesday's Tagesspiegel newspaper, the defense ministers wrote they "share a deep conviction" that European countries need to do more to ensure their own security and aim to build "a stronger Europe within a stronger NATO."

The ministers, however, added that the United States would remain an "indispensable ally."

The pronouncement comes as many in Europe are wary of US President Donald Trump's commitment to the NATO military alliance.

The US leader has threatened to leave the group and to seize control of Greenland, a territory of fellow NATO member Denmark. US presidents have repeatedly called for European NATO members to contribute more to the alliance's military capabilities.

As US support for Ukraine also appears to waver, the five defense ministers reiterated their political, military and financial support for Kyiv as it fights of Russia's full-scale invasion.

In Singapore, to start a four-day business-oriented trip that will also bring him to Japan and South Korea, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said it was up to European and Asian nations to find their spot amid a changing global order.

"We must assert our interests in an international environment shaped by renewed great-power rivalry," Merz said.

With a view to unpredictable tariffs imposed by the United States under President Donald Trump and trade restrictions from China, Merz emphasized the stability offered by Germany and the rest of Europe.

"This is a deliberate counterpoint to what we are currently seeing. We want to do things differently, and we want to show that there is a better way," Merz said, adding that Europe sought to expand partnerships to increase free trade with open competition, reliability and a rules-based order.

He also called for increased international investment and cooperation.

"Under the federal government I lead, investment opportunities will be continuously improved," Merz said following a meeting with Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong. "I encounter a great deal of confidence here in Germany and in Europe as locations for investment."

The German leader called for a new free-trade agreement between the 27-member European Union and the Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), comprising 12 countries across five continents, including Australia, Canada, Japan, Mexico and the United Kingdom. Neither the United States nor China is part of the CPTPP.

For his part, Wong said investment in Germany and Europe would continue.

"Many of our investors, including our sovereign wealth funds, have been investing in Germany for a long time," Wong said. "They will continue to invest because they are confident that, in the long term, Germany and Europe have potential."

Merz and Wong agreed their nations would work to expand cooperation in security and defense as well as trade, investment, sustainable energy and artificial intelligence.

#859. Kylian Mbappé’s China crisis shows how sensitive Mao’s legacy remains | Rebecca Bailey

Real Madrid forward was dropped by brands for comments Chinese media generally steered clear of outlining

It’s been a bad start to the week for the Kylian Mbappé. The France forward missed out on joining the elite roster of Ballon d’Or winners and instead became the latest high-profile addition to a far less illustrious list – that of foreign brands and individuals charged with “hurting the feelings of the Chinese people”.

The saga began when a video of the Real Madrid player making light of a meme involving him and China’s former leader Mao Zedong began spreading.

Within hours Mbappé found himself condemned online, before being unceremoniously dropped by brands, then held responsible for state television suspending the entire top Spanish league from its schedule. On Tuesday Mbappé apologised – “My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China” – as did La Liga, which released a statement saying it “deeply regrets the offence that Kylian Mbappé’s recent comments have caused among Chinese fans”.

Foreign brands from Mercedes to Versace and celebrities from John Cena to Katy Perry have previously been sent to the sin bin for crossing China’s political lines on Tibet, Hong Kong and Taiwan.

Mbappé’s case shows how sensitive Mao’s legacy remains in China 50 years after his death – to the extent that most Chinese coverage of the affair does not even mention what the footballer said.

In the video, Mbappé references a meme of himself and “a guy … I think he was a Chinese dictator”, before a composite image of Mbappé’s face on Mao’s body pops up. (Mbappé has been nicknamed “the dictator” since his time at Paris Saint-Germain, a joke referring to his perceived influence at the club.)

The football app Dongqiudi was among the first to release a statement condemning the “inappropriate remarks”, but said: “Because his comments were offensive to China and the Chinese people, we cannot translate them.” Chinese media have reported on reactions such as the brand desertions, and the China Football Association’s lodging of a “stern protest” with Real Madrid – who apologised on Wednesday “to the Chinese people for any offence caused” – but have generally steered clear of outlining Mbappé’s precise offence.

The topic was still trending on Chinese social media on Wednesday morning, with one hashtag relating to the superstar’s apology boasting more than 600m views. Some posts asked variations on a simple question: “What did he actually say?”

Manya Koetse, editor of the Eye on Digital China newsletter, said in a post on X: “Many netizens without a VPN are still left in the dark about why all the talk about boycotting Mbappé is actually happening.”

Still, many expressed anger at what was characterised as disrespect for, as well as a misunderstanding of, China’s history. “For the majority of the [Chinese] people, Mao was and is still not seen as negatively as it is believed in the west,” said Mobo Gao, professor of Chinese studies at Adelaide University.

Mao was the founding leader of modern China, but his legacy includes radical policies such as the Great Leap Forward, an industrialisation policy blamed for a famine that killed as many as 30 million people by some estimates.

The ruling Communist party (CCP) maintains Mao was a revolutionary hero, though after his death it acknowledged another extreme policy, the violent Cultural Revolution, was a “grave mistake”.

Gao said: “There has been intense tension between Mao hatred and Mao support among the Chinese themselves. This tension is even more keenly felt since the economy has slowed.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Some scholars have pointed to a resurgence of interest in Mao among younger Chinese, with a yearning for a time they regard as more idealistic and egalitarian – something the CCP is keen to keep in check.

Jennifer Pan, professor of communication at Stanford University, said the difficulty of doing independent social science surveys in the past decade meant “our understanding of what Chinese people actually think is weak”. Pan said: “Social media doesn’t fill that gap. It’s noisy, unrepresentative, and censored … What we see is that companies, platforms, broadcasters and the foreign ministry moved together quickly. Did this follow public anger, or did this produce public anger? Either is possible, and we can’t tell which came first.”

Whichever way round, the financial cost for Mbappé is the same. His face is a common sight on Chinese buses, in subways and in online ads, and his commercial deals could be worth “as much as $30m (£22.6m) per year”, said Mark Dreyer, author of Sporting Superpower, a book about China’s ambitions in the sector.

However, “as soon as someone else has decided you’ve crossed the line, it’s a race to who can cut ties quickest, who can be the most patriotic”, he said. “Then you have to kiss the ring – there really is no other way if you want to stay in the market.”

Mbappé’s and La Liga’s swift apologies suggest they are trying to avoid a fate like the NBA, whose lucrative pre-season matches were shut out of China for six years after the Houston Rockets’ then general manager Daryl Morey voiced support for Hong Kong pro-democracy protests in 2019.

La Liga may have better luck, with the state broadcaster CCTV saying it would listen to what Mbappé had to say, and “more importantly” watch what he does.

On Wednesday a foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, said: “We take seriously the apology the individual concerned has made.”

Dreyer said: “It doesn’t sound like it’s an instant ‘all is forgiven’. But it sounds like they’re going to be a little bit more, for want of a better word, reasonable.”

#857. A phone-free Yellow Wall: are Dortmund urging fans to be present or policing them?

It makes sense that sports teams want to keep influencers out of their games. The battle some clubs are waging with their fans, however, is a different dilemma

By all appearances, things on the Yellow Wall seemed as they always had been. The stadium announcer hollered out the first names of Borussia Dortmund’s starting lineup and the supporters responded with their last names, tens of thousands of voices bellowing as one. Dozens of black and yellow flags waved over Europe’s largest standing terrace, a mass of faces fixed on the field beneath them.

And then Signal Iduna Park, sold out with 81,365 fans, roared when Max Beier’s lone goal led Dortmund to victory over Eintracht Frankfurt last Saturday, putting the home side even on points with Bayern Munich atop the Bundesliga standings.

Yet, apparently, a crisis of a sort has been churning just below the surface of what is, by broad consensus, Europe’s best home support.

On Friday, Dortmund had announced a kind of bribery scheme. A rewards program is probably a kinder way of putting it. Fans who stayed off their phones during the bout with Eintracht had the chance to win signed jerseys and earn gift cards to the club’s merchandise store. If they activated a so-called “fan mode” on the club’s app – a name so phenomenally passive-aggressive you can only applaud whoever came up with it – the club could count who unlocked their phones the fewest times during the game. For every minute the fans left their phones alone, they got points.

Dortmund are not the only German team to pick a fight with phones.

Second-division clubs Hertha Berlin and Dynamo Dresden have banned commercial influencer-style videos in their stadiums altogether, fearing for both the integrity of the TV rights they sell and the experience of their fans. Dortmund, likewise, appear motivated by the incursion of influencers, who are siphoning off and monetizing footage of the famous match-day experience and growing into a nuisance for regulars.

This problem has also afflicted the tennis majors. The US Open now resembles an influencer convention more than it does a tennis tournament. When the US Tennis Association credentialed more than 100 content creators this year, the influencers grew so disruptive that a match was stopped when a chair umpire had to ask them to turn off a ring light. Wimbledon has refused to credential influencers for just this reason, which doesn’t stop them from getting in with regular tickets or through sponsors.

Dortmund’s attempt at shaping fan behavior, however, goes further than warding off the cultural content parasites. This please-stop-holding-up-your-phones-and-just-live-in-the-present plea raises quasi-existential questions about sport and its consumption.

“Over 81,000 people in the stadium, singing, cheering, and holding their breath together: this here and now is irreplaceable,” Dortmund chief executive Carsten Cramer said. “And that’s exactly what we’re putting front and center together.”

“Anyone at a soccer game should experience the moment and the emotions – not just a cell phone screen,” added Marcel de Groot, the chief executive of Vodafone Germany, both a cellphone service provider and a Dortmund sponsor. “Let’s leave our smartphones in our pockets more often at the stadium and instead focus on what’s happening on the field and in the stands.”

These were statements delivered with unshakeable confidence in their righteousness, yet there is evidence to suggest this simply isn’t how some fans want to behave at stadiums.

Which begs the question: can, and should, professional sports teams get to dictate how their ticket-buying fans experience their games? It’s surely a question that’s crossed the mind of all the musicians who now perform to a sea of cell phones, their flashlights on, obscuring the faces in the crowd. Did their fans buy the right to experience the concert as they please? Or does this objectify the musicians and diminish the performance, somehow?

It goes back to the question of whether sport is entertainment, and whether its consumers get to sit back and let the proceedings and the attendant stimuli wash over them. Or whether they are something else entirely: active participants in the games they attend. If that is so, then fandom amounts to a parasocial relationship conferring membership to a community with attendant behavioral expectations.

What are the responsibilities of the ticketholder? Do teams get to purity-test their supporters? What do fans owe their teams? Is live soccer just content? A day out, not unlike going to the movies or a museum, where nobody expects total focus and for you to cheer on the thing you’re looking at? Is it heresy to even suggest this?

The latter tends to be the view, or at least the vibe, in most American sports leagues where fans are often less engaged, told by an announcer and a jumbo screen when and what to clap or stomp or chant. This has always contrasted with the feel of global football, where the folklore is usually organic, sparked and dictated by the fans themselves. It’s why all of those pre-game and half-time concerts at the World Cup final rankled, drowning out the thrum of the throaty Argentina fans.

It feels both instructive and fitting that this debate broke out at Dortmund. The Bundesliga’s rules on safeguarding fan majority ownership of very nearly every club have preserved the league as a kind of supporters’ paradise, with relatively cheap tickets and policies that put fans first. Dortmund, for their part, have been held up for years as a paradigm for their following – thus attracting the influencers, of course.

The latter will be dealt with, it seems. In an age when soccer clubs are essentially production houses who also field company teams, it always seemed inevitable that these interlopers would be expelled from the premises. The fans, however, are not so easily corrected on behavior their teams have deemed undesirable. And they will vote with their credit cards.

Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: U.S. Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts, which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.

#855. Why is it going so wrong for Le Bris at Sunderland?

Regis Le Bris - post-match interview - Coventry City v Sunderland

Dinamo Zagreb under the lights at the Stadium of Light on Bonfire Night.

These should be exciting times for Sunderland and their fans, who before this season had been starved of European football for more than half a century.

Instead there is a concern the club's Europa League campaign, which includes a trip to AC Milan in December, has become a hindrance after the team's poor domestic start to the season.

Last season's surprise Premier League package are rooted to the bottom of the table, with just one win and six defeats from nine games.

Will a game against the champions of Croatia on Thursday (20:00 GMT) serve as a welcome distraction before Sunday's visit of Chelsea?

When Sunderland won at Stamford Bridge last season in their ninth game back after promotion, the Black Cats sat second in the table after an electrifying start.

After nine games this season, it is a very different story.

Questions are being asked about the long-term future of manager Regis le Bris - the man who masterminded Sunderland's return to Europe for the first time in 53 years.

So after last season's impressive seventh-placed finish, why are Sunderland struggling this time round?

Following last Saturday's 3-1 defeat at Coventry City, captain Granit Xhaka questioned the team's "courage", weeks after France defender Nordi Mukiele claimed the side had become "arrogant".

BBC Sport understands Le Bris' job is not in immediate danger and he will be given more time to turn things around.

The Frenchman, in charge since July 2024, is Sunderland's longest-serving manager since Steve Bruce, who was in charge between June 2009 and November 2011.

Le Bris has credit in the bank for winning promotion and then claiming a European spot.

This season he has managed to propel the Black Cats into the Carabao Cup quarter-finals, where they face fellow Premier League strugglers Crystal Palace at Selhurst Park.

But how long will Sunderland's hierarchy remain patient if the club, two points from safety, stay anchored in the bottom three?

"They ended last season quite well to get into Europe and that felt really historic," former Sunderland loan signing Nedum Onuoha told BBC Sport.

"But there was talk then that maybe he [Le Bris] wasn't quite the guy.

"Sunderland fans who probably had their doubts last season, I really doubt that they will be thinking he is the manager long term."

French football expert Julien Laurens added about former Lorient boss Le Bris: "This is not looking good.

"I look at Sunderland and I'm not seeing him find the solutions to turn things around. For me that is really worrying."

Sunderland's paradox - San Siro trip amid relegation battle

Sunderland's only Premier League win this season was on 30 August, a 1-0 victory at home to Fulham

Sunderland, who were playing in League One as recently as 2022, were lauded as one of the stories of last season, after doing the double over Chelsea and fierce rivals Newcastle, as well as holding both Arsenal and Manchester City at home.

The numbers suggest repeated success was always going to be difficult.

Only relegated Burnley and Wolves had a lower Expected Goals difference - comparing the amount of good chances created to those chances created against them - than Sunderland last campaign.

How about that dreaded second-season syndrome then. Is it even a thing?

Last season Sunderland and Leeds became the 53rd and 54th promoted sides to survive in the Premier League.

Of the previous 52, only 11 were relegated the following season (21%). The vast majority of promoted teams that stay up do not suffer from second-season syndrome.

With three-quarters of the Premier League season to go, Sunderland will rightly argue there is plenty of time to save themselves.

Yet those heady days of 12 months ago must feel a long way off.

Two of Sunderland's seven league goals this season have come from the penalty spot, while they have finished with 10 men in defeats by Arsenal (Reinildo Mandava sent off), Bournemouth (Kevin Danso sent off) and Coventry (Omar Alderete sent off).

Meanwhile, Sunderland have failed to score a first-half goal in seven of their nine league games.

"Having been promoted many will have believed Sunderland exceeded expectations by finishing in the European places last season," added Onuoha, who made 31 Premier League appearances for the club in 2010-11.

"This season it is five points from nine games with seven goals scored. That speaks for itself in some ways - especially when three of those seven goals came in one game [a 3-5 defeat at Manchester City].

"It doesn't feel at the minute that things are heading in the right direction."

Where is it all going wrong for Sunderland?

Sunderland spent Â£161m on 15 new players after winning promotion to the Premier League in the summer of 2025.

This time round, just Â£60m was invested on five players.

Most fans, however, will have been delighted to keep hold of experienced captain Xhaka and forward Brian Brobbey, who scored seven league goals last season before going on to score three for the Netherlands at the World Cup.

Brobbey, who has signed a new contract until 2031, has yet to score since returning from a hamstring injury, while former Arsenal midfielder Xhaka was downbeat after last weekend's defeat at newly promoted Coventry.

"I don't know exactly what the problem is," said the Switzerland midfielder.

"Is it concentration? Is it other things? We are bottom of the league but in football you need to think positive and to show courage as well.

Carl Jenkinson, who was at Arsenal with Xhaka, told BBC Sport his former team-mate's remarks were "concerning".

"He seemed really deflated and that is very unlike Granit," added the former full-back, who made 41 Premier League appearances for the Gunners between 2011 and 2019.

Laurens said the form of Xhaka and Mukiele, who helped Sunderland towards 11 clean sheets in the top flight last season, had dipped significantly this season.

"They are the leaders and they are way below the levels they had," he added. "The first one to pay the price [for the team's poor form] is usually the manager."

Sunderland are without a win in seven Premier League games

For many, the reason for Sunderland's current struggles appears obvious - the added demand of Europe.

Their first European campaign since 1973 means at least eight games in the Europa League. Unlike in the Premier League, Sunderland have started well in Europe, winning two and drawing one of their first three league phase matches.

"Europe is great," added Laurens. "Sunderland fans will be travelling to Milan, it's wonderful.

"It could be a distraction for the players - especially the ones who have never played in Europe before. It's less time to practise on the training pitch.

"You play Thursday-Sunday and that's a very different dynamic to what Sunderland had last season."

On Wednesday, Le Bris described Sunderland as having "growing pains" this season.

He added: "Is it unexpected? I would say no.

"We are experiencing probably the most demanding challenge Sunderland have ever faced - Premier League, Europa League, quarter-final in the Carabao Cup, FA Cup later.

"It's a new journey - not for everyone because many of our players experienced this situation before, but it's still a new group, one year together.

"I think we are still competitive. We trust our team, our level, but repeating performances is different, this is the new step."

Sunderland have lost two and drawn one of their three Premier League games after playing in Europe.

They could certainly do with beating Chelsea on Sunday after playing Dinamo Zagreb to lift the mood.

Otherwise it is going to be an unhappy international break for Sunderland and their passionate fanbase.

#854. How can playing for Manchester City fit into Marc Guéhi’s moral universe? | Barney Ronay

Club’s predicament raises interesting questions about principles, both for individuals and the Premier League

I felt unbelievably ponderous. My head was made of Aztec stone. I realised I didn’t want to be with all these people. Somebody came at me, a huge individual in silver and blue. I fell at his feet and grabbed one shoe. I started untying the lace. He kicked away from me. I got up and walked off. I was exceedingly hungry.

Not my words. Also not the words of the Manchester City centre-back Marc Guéhi, despite what you were thinking there. This is instead a condensed quote from the mind of Gary Harkness, existentially curious college running-back and the narrator of Don DeLillo’s great American football novel End Zone.

This passage describes a moment where Gary plays a game having been urged by his friends to smoke pot beforehand to discover whether it improves his understanding of time and space, or just makes him want to lie down and untie someone’s laces. It marks a turning point for Gary. To this point football has been a comforting world. He sees clarity in its militaristic rituals, finds in sport “the illusion that order is possible”, hears hidden truths in the coaches’ shouted instructions. Button up. Get fetal. Get fetal. Get fetal. Run with reckless abandon.

Now the illusion has collapsed. Gary walks off the football field and begins instead to fixate on cold war fears and nuclear apocalypse. Death and political power have entered the chat.

Now, I’m not saying Marc Guéhi is Gary Harkness. You might be saying that. That’s your choice. But Guéhi has seemed a bit distracted in the last few weeks. Oddly for an agile and technically sound centre-back, he has seemed brittle and absent, vulnerable to being pressed.

There have been a couple of things said about City’s players in this regard. The first is that their minds might not be wholly on the game, that in the middle of a game against Croatia, for example, concerned only with manoeuvring through tiny pockets of space, Nico O’Reilly is also thinking: “Hmm, but how is it possible even by omission to honestly contravene rules E.3 and E.4 which state clearly that …oh. Wait, no. Oh dear.”

Football doesn’t work like this. The physical game is a place of total focus. But still, nothing is watertight. And this speaks to the second thing people have said, repeated like an absolute truth, that the players are entirely separate from all this. They cannot be questioned here, or indeed expected to ask questions of their own. The players are simply avatars, employees, free from any kind of agency. Players don’t have access to Google. They cannot make moral judgments. And yes, this may not be true of any other human in any other field. It may be the case that elite footballers are in fact unusually empowered, free to do whatever they want. But the consensus is clear. It is not a footballer’s business to have opinions on their employers, or what happens out of their line of vision.

This does help to avoid some tricky conundrums. Guéhi, for example, is a man of absolute public principle. Fair enough. I respect his willingness to resist popular pressure and personalise his support for the rainbow armband by writing things about Jesus on top of it. This is living your values. It’s free speech, figuring out your own moral universe. Doing so by following the absolute tenets of his religion. Go for it.

At the same time, Guéhi is playing for a club that has been convicted of cheating and lying. People are free to disagree with the rules. But if others are sticking to them, this amounts to deceit, stolen win bonuses, stolen glory. And the Bible is very clear on this. Thessalonians 4:6: “No one should transgress and defraud his brother.” Proverbs 20:17: “Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be full of gravel.” Now, I don’t believe these words to be divinely ordained. They’re great words. Totally dig the vibe. But Guéhi does believe these things to be an absolute instruction. How does this fit together in his head? How does that gravel (pending appeal) taste right now?

Again, fine if you can square it. It’s a personal journey. Park the apparent moral dilemma. See if your legal team can come up with a better final outcome. But things have changed in one significant way since the verdict dropped, an element that is now unchallenged, and which has been largely unremarked in the middle of the chaos. Understandably so. This stuff is gruelling. Everyone just wants to watch some football in the brief lull between legal rage events. But there are two points worth making in the interim. The second of which is an admission that affects many other things.

The first issue is: do you actually understand the basis of the Manchester City appeal? That evidence has seemingly been leaked. The irrefutable body of evidence, Body Of Evidence 2, the long-awaited tribunal-based Madonna erotic thriller vehicle, contains a vital detail: the additional money in City’s coffers, almost a billion, did not come from the owners, the Abu Dhabi United Group, which is owned, like City, by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan. This would be against the rules. It came instead from the Abu Dhabi government, which is essentially the Abu Dhabi royal family, of which Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan is a member; as he is also, wearing a different hat, of the Abu Dhabi government.

And maybe this means it’s fine. It seems the government often tops up the sponsor companies like a benevolent uncle. In the period the charges relate to there was no need for sponsor deals to be of market value, as there is now. So if we accept all this, if we can establish a binding principle of wearing different hats in different rooms, this may be a way out. Maybe.

This is a familiar concept in the high court, in an age of shell companies and tricky fiscal flows. Mega-million cases hang on whether ownership really is separate, or whether this is, to echo a phrase, a sham process. The person on the Clapham omnibus might not buy any of this. Do these really seem like separate entities? Or a bit like adopting a French accent when the bailiffs ring up and maintaining that, no, Monsieur Ronay is not here, and he definitely doesn’t run this dry cleaners. That, instead, is me.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

If you make the case you win the case. This is all in the end about the application of rules, and that is a good thing. But the key point here is the secondary issue derived from this. City’s leaked defence, in making their case, is also saying, without pretence or mucking about, that the club is indeed funded by the Abu Dhabi government. This is something City’s fans have at times weirdly denied. But we have it in plain sight now, not just admitted but insisted on. The ultimate source of the dizzying success of the club that has defined a Premier League era is the government. Guéhi is, in effect, an Abu Dhabi civil servant. Perhaps the United Arab Emirates national team should have six stars on their jersey, one for each Premier League won. But there is no way of covering your ears now. City actively want us to accept this.

What are the consequences of this new fact? It comes with two urgent questions. The first is the moral one. Back again to Guéhi as the best example. This is what he is promoting here. And Guéhi is a man entirely guided by the principles of his faith. A private matter perhaps, except that it’s not, because Guéhi’s church explicitly orders its members to go out and proselytise. Guéhi is a member of Ballers in God, which actively tries to awaken Christian faith in the dressing room. He plays with Christian messages on his matchday kit intended to make you, the reader, think yes, maybe I too should follow this evangelical church.

And here is the key thing. This is a criminal offence in Abu Dhabi. Under UAE penal code, giving out Christian leaflets will get you arrested. A Christian pastor in the UAE was sentenced to a year in prison for giving a Muslim a Bible. Some Americans were deported for giving out Christian literature in the Dubai shopping district. Spreading the gospel, which Guéhi is morally bound to do, is illegal in the place that pays his direct employers.

Are players just avatars, empty shells? How much do you really believe in this? These are, more than ever, very interesting questions. And they don’t just apply to issues of personal principle.

The regulator now has this information, too. Abu Dhabi funded the purchase of Nolito. Abu Dhabi dictated the flow of English football finance. The same pocket that paid for this is also funding at arm’s length the civil war in Sudan, the hospital massacres, the piles of bodies so high they can be seen from satellite imaging. Abu Dhabi, which criminalises homosexuality, which crushes dissent, is openly identifying itself as the mega-funder of a Premier League club. Is this a fit and proper influence?

There are very obvious reasons why this is not desirable. Governments spy and wage war and break rules. They have a sacred trust to promote their own interests by any means necessary. It is hard to see how this kind of owner fits the regulatory framework. Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund had to twirl through semantic hoops when buying Newcastle to establish it was an entity at one remove from a government, as opposed to a government entity. In making the opposite case for their funding City have not only exposed their own live-your-values central defender, they have put themselves in a place where, even if you win on one front, you’ve started to look like a very strange presence.

This deserves to be unravelled in all its wider implications. It may be the biggest issue here, whatever the final verdict. How can this be the right thing? How can City’s fans look their own autocratic government-funded club in the eye? The quiet thing has been said out loud. And its implications are bigger than the game, bigger than legal opinion. Enough, perhaps to make you question the existential point of this thing, where the best course of action really might be to walk off and look for the nearest cheeseburger.

#853. Harry Kane: Ballon d’Or for Bayern Munich striker

Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane has won football's most prestigious individual prize, beating Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal. Kane has developed even more in the Bundesliga despite an uneven league.

To most Bayern Munich fans under the age of 40, Karl-Heinz Rummenigge was the club CEO who regularly spoke his mind. Fans with longer memories, or a better grasp of Bavarian football history, recall Rummenigge as one of the club's all-time great players. He was also the last Bayern man to win the Ballon d'Or — in 1981. The last Bundesliga player to win was Borussia Dortmund's Matthias Sammer, in 1996.

That long drought ended on Monday, with Harry Kane, born 12 years after Rummenigge's win, picking up the 2026 trophy at a ceremony held, as a one-off, in his native London.

"I am almost speechless. Being here in London has made it extra special,” he said on stage.

Not many people would have thought it, and maybe even I wouldn't have thought I'd be this far," Kane later told British sports streaming plaftorm DAZN.

Lamine Yamal, the prodigious Barcelona and Spain forward who won the Euros at 16, finished third. At the end of the 2025-26 season, on which the award is judged, Yamal won the World Cup with Spain as well as the La Liga title. Kylian Mbappe came in second.

Kane's 73 goals for club and country last season made for a strong case, and the Bundesliga's most expensive signing of all time has already racked up 156 goals in 159 games for the serial German champions. But it's not just the numbers that tell the story, according to his club coach.

"People in England saw him as a goalscorer during his time playing there," Vincent Kompany said of Kane last season. "We've seen other qualities too, such as his footballing intelligence. We can appreciate that now — it was perhaps somewhat underestimated in England. He's like a fine wine that improves with age. I also enjoy that aspect of his game."

Kane continues to improve at 33, a point when many footballers start to regress. Though he is helped by being more reliant on guile and technique than pace, Kane's professionalism is key to staying at the top, according to his Bayern teammate Serge Gnabry.

"He always has the right attitude, always leads the way and sets the tone," Gnabry said ahead of Bayern's 2-2 draw in the Champions League against Arsenal last week. "He never strays from his path, helps the team with his performance and is a top-tier player."

Kane scored a penalty in that match and provided a sensational pass from which Alphonso Davies scored Bayern's opener, another reminder of his all-round game. "The pass was one of my best ones," Kane said after the match. "I knew Phonzy [Davies] would be able to get there with his speed. Whatever I can do to help the team, I'll do. At the moment, it seems to be with assists more than goals."

That attitude has been with Kane from the start. His first-ever coach, Dave Bricknell, from Ridgeway Rovers, an amateur club in northeast London, told DW after Kane joined Bayern from Spurs in 2023: "Harry's mentality is his greatest strength. He doesn't let anything worry him. If he misses a chance, he doesn't care — he will go and score from another chance."

His England coach, Thomas Tuchel, has also emphasized Kane's leadership. "He is the first one to push everyone, and that is his mindset, and he became a very, very hardworking forward on top of his finishing skills, Tuchel said in September as Kane extended his England goal-scoring record against the Czech Republic. "He is a complete package."

There are detractors who point to perceived "stat-padding," or scoring against inferior opponents in international qualifiers and in the Bundesliga, where there are fewer elite teams and a lot less money, than in England. Though Kane's ratio of 213 goals in 320 games in the Premier League is a little off his Bundesliga stats, it bears comparison with any other player in the history of the league.

Kane winning the award is also a boost in profile for the Bundesliga, which has been unable to keep pace, both commercially and on the pitch, with other top European leagues of late, particularly the Premier League and La Liga.

Winning it in a league outside of England or Spain perhaps makes Kane's feat even greater. Other than Ousmane Dembele, who won it last year after Paris Saint-Germain's Champions League win, and Lionel Messi, a serial Ballon d'Or winner, the last player to take the Ballon d'Or for a season played outside England or Spain was was Kaka at AC Milan in 2007, when Italy's Serie A was considered a stronger league.

Kane's career hasn't been straightforward, something he admitted in his speech. After signing his first senior contract with Spurs in July 2010, he was sent out on various loans to lower league sides between 2011-2013 without ever making a huge impression.

"My journey wasn't straightforward. I wasn't the kid who went straight to the top. I had to experience the downs, I had a lot of loan moves, I had to fight my way to be the very best right now, and I hope that can give you determination as well," Kane said in his speech.

For former teammate Jermain Defoe, who also coached Kane at Spurs, those experiences were formative.

"You have to show a resilience. It's not easy when you go out on loan, it can feel like you're being rejected by the club that you are at, which isn't the case," he told DW in 2023, before adding that Kane's ability was always clear.

"When he joined up with the [Tottenham] first team, you could see the potential," Defoe said. "He was always a good finisher, always hit the ball clean. … With Harry you already knew, he had that natural instinct and always felt comfortable in front of goal."

Those goals have, after a failure to win a trophy in England, led to two Bundesliga titles and a German Cup. But success with England remains elusive after a 2026 World Cup exit in the semifinals. Kane will be 35 by the time of the next Euros, in the UK and Ireland in 2028, and has a deal with Bayern until the following year. His form since joining Bayern suggests that he could get better still.

This article was first published on October 22, 2026. It was updated on October 27 after Harry Kane won the 2026 Ballon d'Or.

#851. Unai Simón caps myth-making week with another extraordinary night | Sid Lowe

Athletic’s win over Real Sociedad was culmination of six unique days for the Spain keeper after night at the Palladium

For the third time in six days everyone got to their feet to hand a standing ovation to Unai Simón, dressed in all black, before the world. Named the best men’s goalkeeper on the planet, holding the Lev Yashin trophy, they had applauded him at the London Palladium on Monday night and before the game began at San Mamés, Bilbao, on Sunday. Now somewhere in the middle of it all, the ferocity of the 197th Basque derby, there was another moment, even more meaningful and more lasting, a cheer again giving way to something deeper: an appreciation for a man as well as his work closing a week that will be forever his. Which means it will be forever theirs too.

Real Sociedad and Athletic Club had been doing battle for 72 minutes and it was 2-1 when Simon took off to make a save that denied Carlos Soler an equaliser and defied belief. As the ball flew off his palm, San Mamés exploded. And then it happened: never mind that Athletic still had a derby to win and a corner to defend, forget the fact that the lead was a single goal, the visitors relentless now and 25 minutes still to resist; at the stadium everyone calls the Cathedral, a place of ritual and liturgy like no other, the entire congregation, 50,092 people, started clapping. Started and did not stop. For a minute, maybe more, it was like the match that matters most didn’t matter at all, momentarily fading until it was just him and them together.

That was just one of four superb stops that Simón made as Athletic ended La Real’s four-derby winning run, those saves and goals from Iñaki Williams first and Álex Berenguer giving them a 2-1 win. There had been a six-minute period in the first half alone, immediately after Luka Sucic had made it 1-1, in which he saved from Ander Barrenetxea on 33, Sucic on 34, and Mikel Oyarzabal on 38, then gave everyone a coronary when he dropped a shoulder and dribbled past Oyarzabal on 40. But this, the last of them on 72, was the best; it was also the culmination of an extraordinary night and a six unique days, the kind myths are made of. “We already knew. If anyone [else] had any questions about the trophy, those can be put aside now,” said Athletic’s coach, Edin Terzic. But it was not really the fact that Simon had taken the trophy; it was how he had, when he had.

On Monday, Simon had boarded a Vueling flight from Bilbao for the Ballon d’Or ceremony. A World Cup winner, a tournament record breaker too – albeit one who that day in New Jersey said: “If my gloves could talk they would say they didn’t have to do much” – he knew there was a chance of winning the goalkeeper’s award. For a few weeks, he had wondered what he might say, ordering his thoughts as he drove into Lezama each morning as he had been doing virtually every day for 15 years. By the time he took to the Palladium stage, he knew. Delivered with a light in his eye and without notes, with a steady voice, the speech was 491 words long and lasted two minutes and 21 seconds.

It was also perfect. Spain was taken by it, this abnormal normality: an expression of a man, a perfectly out of place, somehow different to its sport, its society even. It is not unusual to thank people, no, but there was nothing hysterical, nothing Hollywood about this, no posturing, no self indulgence, the only celebration that of a culture. Instead, there was an understated authenticity, gratitude to his cuadrilla, the lifelong mates who are still there, making light of it all; the partner who is an “oasis of calm”, which he knows he needs in this game; the parents who guided him; the goalkeepers who shared the World Cup with him and the friends – Óscar De Marcos, Iñigo Lekue and Gorka Guruzeta – who are about the least footballer footballers you could wish to meet.

To José Ángel Iribar, the legendary Athletic goalkeeper whose statue stands outside San Mamés and whose presence is felt everywhere inside, in whose honour they wear black. To Koldo Asua, the coach who told the boy arriving in Bilbao to leave his ego behind, that what truly matters is the human legacy you leave not the trophies you take: to be remembered as good people. To all those who, he said, had taught him to love a club, to the fans above all.

This is Simón’s ninth season in the first team at Athletic, who he joined at 14. He might not have had any. In the summer of 2018, aged 21 and fourth choice, he went on loan to Elche. But then Chelsea signed Kepa Arrizabalaga. Iago Herrerín got injured. And negotiations over a contract renewal with Álex Remiro stalled, Athletic refusing to play him and eventually losing him to la Real. So they called Elche and asked for their goalkeeper back. “Sometimes you need some luck; that was mine,” Simón says. He hadn’t played a competitive game for Elche; within three days he had played his first for Athletic. He has played almost 300 since, nowhere he would rather be. “In the first few years we had to eat shit, we had bad moments. But even then – even then – there’s something,” he says.

Villarreal 0-1 Espanyol, Levante 0-2 Atlético Madrid, Rayo 3-0 Celta, Betis 2-1 Málaga, Barcelona 6-1 Alavés, Getafe 3-1 Sevilla, Racing Santander 0-3 Real Madrid, Elche 0-1 Valencia, Athletic 2-1 Real Sociedad

As for the good moments, those are unmatched. The five days after Athletic won the Copa del Rey in 2024 were the best of our lives, he said. Yes, even more than those that followed winning the World Cup. And although he was undisputed first choice, he hadn’t even won the Copa del Rey: instead, he was on the bench guiding Julen Agirrezabala, the substitute handed cup games, through the shootout that won their only major trophy in 40 years. When he won the Zamora award as La Liga’s best goalkeeper that season, the first in 50 years since Iribar, the head coach Ernesto Valverde impressed upon him that this mattered – for the club. One of the best things about winning Euro 2024 with Spain, he said, was that it shows academy kids that you can be at clubs like Athletic, that you didn’t need to leave – something he extended to his friend Oyarzabal at Real Sociedad, a man very like he is, silent even in success. Especially in success. Now he had been named the world’s best goalkeeper, an ovation greeting the final Eskerrik asko denoi: “thank you, everyone”. No one foresaw him being the moment of the night, but here he was. Questioned for so long, embraced now.

And here he was back at San Mamés six days later. Here they all were, the timing as impeccable as the performance, the calendar kind. The derby. The derby, unlike any other: all about identity, belonging, tradition. Real Sociedad, led out by Oyarzabal. And on the 50th anniversary of the most emblematic derby moment of them all. In 1976, captains Inaxio Kortabarria and Iribar had walked out at Atotxa together carrying the Ikurriña, the still illegal Basque flag. On Sunday, now 76 and 83 respectively, they led the way out again, handed a guard of honour and carrying an Ikurriña. The original, sewn by the sister of Real’s José Angel de la Hoz Uranga and smuggled into the ground, waited in a frame on the halfway line. San Mamés, blue and white shirts in among the red as ever, applauded them on.

Simón followed Iribar out, he too handed a guard of honour. Oyarzabal, Remiro and all his opponents, clapped him on. The goalkeepers from Athletic’s academy, in black tops, No 1 on the back, held a giant tarpaulin shirt. Unique in the team, it read. There was an ovation then. And then, an hour and a half later, another one: as if Simón was walking off, his work done, when in fact they were in the middle of it all still. When at last it was over, a win secured, he listened to the players and fans sing Mikel Laboa’s Txoria txori together, a song of freedom. “It’s lovely,” he said. “Because they identify with this team, they’re proud of us.”

Of all the nights, Simón had chosen this one to produce probably the performance of his life. “Enormous”, Sport called him; “gigantic”, El Mundo Deportivo said. Even Real’s Jon Aramburu, still angry at the penalty he was judged to have committed on Nico Williams from which Berenguer made it 2-1, said: “That’s why he won the trophy.” The opener, made by Williams and scored by Williams, Nico releasing Iñaki, was superb. On another intense, enjoyable night, described by the referee – they’re doing post-game interviews now – as “a typical derby: hard but noble too”, plenty played well. But no one got near to Simón, man of the match by a mile. “What a goalkeeper you have!” Terzic was told. “The best in the world,” he said.

#850. Real Madrid reach verbal agreement to sign Gabriel

JJ Gabriel joined Manchester United in 2022

Real Madrid are confident of winning the race to sign Manchester United forward JJ Gabriel after reaching a verbal agreement with the teenager.

The 16-year-old is registered at United, but has not been back to the club since walking out in September.

Gabriel, who played against Atletico Madrid on United's pre-season tour, had been expected to become the club's youngest debutant in September's Carabao Cup tie against Brighton.

However, he has opted to look elsewhere for senior football and has been training on his own in Spain.

His availability alerted clubs around Europe, including Barcelona and Paris St-Germain, but Real now expect to sign the youngster in January.

Though no club-to-club talks have been held, sources have told BBC Sport Real have verbally agreed a deal with Gabriel and his representatives.

Gabriel, who scored a hat-trick on his Uefa Youth League debut, has secured a European Union passport, which is expected to make it easier for him to sign for a club outside England.

United would be due compensation should Gabriel leave, although the figure will be lower if he signs for a club outside the Premier League.

He was named the Premier League's Under-18 player of the season last term, despite being only 14 when the season campaign.

"The best 15-year-old in Europe," was how Gabriel was described by a United source this year, while former interim manager Darren Fletcher said: "The world is his oyster."

Speaking after the EFL Cup defeat by Brighton, United head coach Michael Carrick said: "We've got to be really careful of the whole situation.

"He's a young boy...from a club point of view, looking after our younger players - their welfare, their well-being, their exposure - we've got to be really conscious of that in this situation."

#847. Roster rifts, police raids and Son’s uncertain future leave South Korea at a crossroads

After a disaster World Cup, the team have continued to spiral, with tensions high between young and older players and the captain’s standing in question

Son Heung-min and Cristiano Ronaldo are iconic No 7s, Premier League legends and international record-breakers. Now there is a surprising danger of them having something else in common: being a divisive presence in their national teams.

On 21 October, during a parliamentary committee meeting, politician Jeong Yeon-wook put a question to acting Korea Football Association (KFA) president Lee Yong-soo, that took a story out of the sports pages and into the national conversation. “It is said that recently, within the national team squad, players have been calling him not by his name but as ‘No 7’ or ‘that person’. Do you know who that is?” Lee then replied, “Are you referring to Son Heung-min?” Jeong went on: “So it appears to be true. … It has also been revealed that the national team’s leadership is causing discord and has broken down overall.” Lee declined to comment.

How has it come to this? Less than 18 months ago, Son was lifting the Europa League trophy as Tottenham Hotspur captain. That was his last act for the London club after a decade in the Premier League, during which he became a face of the world’s most popular domestic league and a huge star back home. Then came a move to Los Angeles FC in Major League Soccer, one the 34-year-old said was made partly to prepare for the 2026 World Cup.

That tournament was a disaster, with a group-stage exit and a media boycott after unnamed reporters had mocked Son’s lack of military service. He started on the bench for the final game, a dismal defeat to South Africa. Since then, coach Hong Myung-bo and KFA president Chung Mong-gyu stepped down, were grilled by parliamentarians and then police raided KFA offices. All agree that it was a terrible summer for Korean soccer, but that seems to be where the shared opinions end.

Divisions between older and younger players are not uncommon in soccer but Korea’s situation is unusually complex. A colleague just a year older is addressed differently and with deference. Guus Hiddink saw this as an issue when he arrived as national team coach in 2001, famously forcing players to sit together when eating in a bid to make it possible for the juniors to shout instructions at their seniors during games.

This seems more serious – even more than at the Asian Cup in 2024 when there was an altercation over table tennis between Son and a group of younger players including rising star Lee Kang-in that resulted in the skipper dislocating a finger. Lee and Son soon made up but there is a bigger issue now. According to many reports, the class of 1996 are unhappy. Kim Min-jae of Bayern Munich, FC Porto’s Hwang In-beom and Hwang Hee-chan, formerly of Wolverhampton Wanderers and now with Schalke 04, are all now senior players and, it seems, unhappy with the leadership in the team and after the World Cup wanted a fresh start with a new captain and new head coach.

But with interim Robert Moreno appointed in September until the end of November – the federation also has no president at the moment – Korean soccer is in a holding pattern. The Asian Cup, a tournament that the Taeguk Warriors have not won since 1960, is just weeks away.

“I’m tired physically and mentally,” Hwang In-beom said after a 0-0 draw with Venezuela on 2 October. “It’s been about nine years since I joined the national team, and from then until now, there are many things that need to change, in football and in many other areas, but it doesn’t seem to be happening.” At the same time Kim Min-jae complained about some in the team not pulling their weight. “Everyone needs to fight and compete together, but we didn’t do that. Look at our defenders; I felt sorry for them.”

As the window ended, there were reports that the three were ready to quit the national team before being persuaded not to by a KFA official – reports not denied by the association.

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

Fans have become frustrated at such stories and the oblique comments with no one actually stepping forward to say what the problems are and how they want them to be solved. Son is still popular in Korea, despite having left the country at 16, but his relationship with the media is not the same as that of his national team peers. Some fans believe that some reporters are stirring the pot in revenge for the media boycott at the World Cup.

Still, there is no denying that, at 34, Son is no longer an elite-level forward. There are still great moments, such as a free-kick against Uzbekistan on 6 October to score his 59th international goal, the most of any South Korean. There has long been a debate about Son’s best role in the national team – out wide or in the middle – but it is no longer unthinkable that the discussion will move towards whether he should start at all.

Unlike Ronaldo, Son does not seem the type to hang around until the bitter end or release lengthy statements. The 2030 World Cup is unlikely but helping the team win the Asian Cup, which is scheduled to kick off 7 January, would be a fine legacy. There is also the chance the tournament is delayed until 2028 due to Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. That could be a blessing in disguise, to allow a divided team to come together, or the situation, bad as it already is, could become worse.

#846. Serbian police shoot dead assailant at Israeli Embassy

A "minor" has been killed by police after attacking a guard at Israel's embassy in Belgrade with knives, the interior minister says. Ivica Dacic said police had declared the highest terror alert after the incident.

A knife-wielding assailant attacked a police guard outside the Israeli Embassy in the Serbian capital, Belgrade, overnight to Wednesday, slightly wounding the officer before being shot dead by him, Serbia's interior minister said.

Interior Minister Ivica Dacic said the attacker, whom he described as a minor, had been monitored by security agencies as a supporter of the terrorist organization "Islamic State" (IS).

Israel's Foreign Ministry later confirmed an "attempted terrorist attack" near its embassy in Belgrade, adding that no personnel were injured and the incident was being investigated.

The attacker was thought to come from the western Serbian town of Sabac and "kept the black flag in support of the 'Islamic State' on his Instagram” account," according to the minister.

Dacic said the assailant shouted "Allahu Akbar," or "God is great" in Arabic, during the attack on the guard. According to Dacic, the guard killed the attacker in self-defense.

He said police were treating the incident as a terrorist attack, with the terrorism threat level raised to its highest, or "red alert."

"This means tighter security checks and an increased police presence at sensitive sites, including infrastructure facilities and places where large crowds gather," he said.

The attack came  just days after key early parliamentary election in Serbia and one day after Israel held its parliamentary vote, with no clear result yet in sight.

In June 2024, an attacker with a crossbow seriously wounded a Serbian police officer guarding the same embassy in Belgrade before being shot and killed by police.

That attacker was identified as a 25-year-old Islamic convert from a village near the capital who had become radicalized.

#845. An island in mourning: Tenerife processes death of De Miguel

Fans have been paying their respects to Tenerife's Jesus de Miguel following his death on Tuesday

As you arrive on the holiday island of Tenerife, there is a profound sense of grief, pain and disbelief at the death of footballer Jesus de Miguel.

The Canary island is in mourning for the Tenerife striker, who died from injuries sustained in a collision with FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono during a match on Monday.

The 30-year-old had quickly established himself as a club favourite, scoring 11 goals in his first season as Tenerife were promoted to the second tier of Spanish football.

But now the Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez Stadium has become a shrine to the player, with hundreds of people gathering throughout the past few days to lay flowers, light candles and pay their respects.

Bouquets, rosettes sent by clubs from across Spain, prayer cards, photographs, children's drawings and scarves have been laid around the grounds outside gate nine.

It is a deeply moving scene. Fans and residents stand in silence, taking in the tributes.

Many are visibly tearful as the scale of the loss begins to sink in at the very place the incident happened.

'Most difficult days of my life' for keeper Owono

Among those paying their respects were Lisa and Lee, visiting Tenerife from Stoke-on-Trent.

They had arrived on holiday at the weekend and decided to attend Monday's match, hoping to experience Spanish football for the first time.

"We never expected something like this to happen," they told BBC Sport.

"We knew it was serious when the players surrounded him [De Miguel], but to see players crying and actually praying on the pitch was very emotional.

"When we found out the news the next day, it just really hit us."

The couple described the atmosphere inside the stadium as sombre and almost completely silent as spectators waited to understand what was happening.

"You always expect somebody to pull through," Lee said. "And then seeing the news the next day, it was just unbelievable."

They returned to the stadium on Wednesday to lay a Port Vale shirt among the tributes, wanting to show their support for the Tenerife community.

"Football has no colours," Lisa said. "If it was one of our players, we'd be heartbroken. They're part of your family."

For Carlos, a player with Tenerife's disability side Tenerife Foundation, the loss is particularly personal.

"Honestly, there are no words to describe him. He was incredible," Carlos said as he lay a flag on the ground.

He described De Miguel as a figure who had helped shape the club's recent history.

"He practically gave his heart and soul for the shirt. He's already a legend at the club because, after all, we were in a very difficult position a few years ago and he helped pull us out of it.

"Without him, I don't think we would be where we are today."

Carlos was at Monday's match and said he was left in shock by what unfolded.

"When I left the stadium I was trembling and I continued to feel that way for hours.

"Right now, we're incredibly hurt and very sad. I also want to send my support to his family, who I can only imagine must be absolutely devastated."

English fans in Tenerife pay tribute to De Miguel

The sense of loss has extended far beyond the stadium.

Poli Suarez, the Canary Islands' minister for education and sport, said Tenerife was in "complete mourning".

"Canarian sport has been left devastated," Suarez told BBC Sport. "The club is broken. Absolutely heartbroken."

Suarez also stressed that the thoughts of everyone were with De Miguel's wife, daughter and wider family.

"They are the ones suffering most directly from this loss, just as the Tenerife supporters are suffering," he said.

The government has pledged its support to the club, players and supporters, with Suarez describing De Miguel as a footballer who had become part of the Canary Islands' sporting history.

"The loss of Jesus de Miguel is now part of our history," Suarez said.

"Not only because of the circumstances of his death, but also because of the affection he always showed towards our island and towards his club."

A further tribute is planned for Saturday at 18:00 GMT, with supporters encouraged to come together to honour his memory.

"It will be an opportunity to show our affection and emotion, and to demonstrate our solidarity with the family," Suarez said.

"We want to show all our affection for Jesus de Miguel."
