#834. ‘Historic change’: what the 2026 US mid-term election results mean for science

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Paediatrician Annie Andrews, a Democrat, won a US Senate seat in South Carolina in a surprise victory on 3 November. Democrats had not won a Senate seat in the state since 1998.Credit: Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty

The US mid-term elections swept the Democratic party to power in both chambers of the US Congress, raising hopes that lawmakers will now push back against disruptions to science introduced by the administration of Republican President Donald Trump.

The results will mark the end of nearly two years in which the Republicans controlled the presidency and both congressional chambers — and many scientists around the world are celebrating the change as an opportunity to protect the country’s research system.

How the US mid-term elections could shake up science

How the US mid-term elections could shake up science

“This is a big win,” says Megan Peters, a cognitive scientist who moved in 2025 from the University of California Irvine to University College London in part because of worries about US science. “It’s a demonstration that US [voters] are dissatisfied with what the current administration has been doing.” Scientific research “is America’s superpower, and it’s been cut at the knees”.

Those hopeful for change include researchers affected by the shuttering of the US Agency for International Development (USAID) early in Trump’s presidency. “I’m cautiously optimistic,” says Quarraisha Abdool Karim, an epidemiologist at the Centre for the AIDS Programme of Research in Durban, South Africa, which had partnered with USAID on clinical trials. “What we’ve seen in the past 24 hours is that democracy and democratic principles, with individuals turning out to vote, can make a huge difference.” But, she adds, “we will not see overnight changes”.

As of 2.15 p.m. EST on 4 November, Democrats had secured at least 237 seats in the 435-seat US House of Representatives and 54 seats in the 100-member US Senate, giving them decisive majorities in both, with votes still being counted in some states. These majorities will give them the power to craft legislation that counteracts Trump’s science agenda, although there will still be obstacles. For instance, given that Democrats haven’t won two-thirds of the seats in either chamber of Congress, the president can veto those bills.

Trump initially told The New York Times that he would accept the mid-term election results and that he would “look forward” to working with Democrats. Later, however, he posted an image of a red hat with the word ‘VETO’ to Truth Social, his social media platform.

Since Donald Trump became president for the second time in January 2025, his administration has pushed for unprecedented cuts to science funding, politicised decision-making at federal science agencies and interfered with policies at US universities that receive federal funding.

When Democrats take charge of both chambers of the US Congress on 3 January 2027, they will be able to take charge of congressional committees, including science committees; set agendas for hearings that investigate government officials and their science policies; and use legally binding subpoenas to compel the Trump administration to provide documents and testify in front of Congress.

‘Science needs defending’: record number of researchers run for office in US mid-terms

‘Science needs defending’: record number of researchers run for office in US mid-terms

On social media, Democrats promised to make use of that authority. Robert Garcia, a representative from California who will soon chair the House Oversight Committee, shared a two-word statement aimed at the Trump administration: “Lawyer up.” In particular, scientists are calling for scrutiny of Russell Vought, director of the White House Office of Management and Budget, who has drafted a plan that gives political appointees, rather than scientist peer reviewers, control of decisions about research grants, and who has delayed the distribution of congressionally-approved science funds.

Scientists and policy specialists said they were hoping to see more congressional oversight of the actions of Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the head of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) who has questioned vaccine safety and whose tenure has coincided with the country’s worst measles resurgence in decades. “For sure, Secretary Kennedy will be put on the hot seat” to explain his actions, which have been unscientific, says Georges Benjamin, executive director of the American Public Health Association in Washington DC. “What I’m hoping is that Congress will really push this administration to have a much more proactive response to the measles epidemic.”

Zoe Lofgren, a Democratic representative from California, said she would campaign to become the head of the House Science, Space and Technology Committee, which oversees agencies such as NASA and the US National Science Foundation. “We will hold this administration accountable for the damage they have done to the American scientific enterprise,” she said in a statement.

Stand Up for Science (SUFS), a science-advocacy group based in Atlanta, Georgia that has organized protests against the Trump administration’s reshaping of US science, says that it will release a plan on 5 November with strategies to push Congress for change.

Whether Congress will be able to increase funding for federal science, rather than just hold it relatively steady as they have for the past two years, is doubtful, however. Susan Collins, a Republican senator from Maine and chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, had protected science budgets but she lost her re-election bid last night. Large boosts to science spending could also just be difficult to pass, given that the budget must also be signed by Trump, who has tried to slash non-defence science spending.

#831. Russia in Africa: What is Putin hoping to achieve?

Following its invasion of Ukraine and the resulting rift with the West, Russia has declared that it intends to make a "historic return" to Africa. What have we seen of this so far?

The conflict with the West sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine  prompted Russian President Vladimir Putin to seek support from other parts of the world. Africa has become a focus, with foreign minister Sergei Lavrov visiting the continent increasingly often.

Russian foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova has described it as a "historic return," and declared no one and nothing could be compared to what Russia did for Africa in the 20th century.

A Russia-Africa summit has been held in Russia at roughly three-year intervals since 2019. The third takes place in Moscow on October 28 and 29. The program focusses on economic cooperation. Other topics range from politics and security to science and culture. But Russia is actively working with only a few African countries, mainly in the north of the continent, and this is reflected in the trade figures.

"South Africa is still Africa's largest national economy, but its volume of trade with Russia is small, far less than with Egypt and Algeria," says Ivan Klyszcz from the International Centre for Defence and Security (ICDS) in Tallinn, Estonia.

"Egypt and Algeria in particular are key partners for Russia. Egypt plays an important role in this regard. Russian diplomats and business representatives are trying to extend relationships with other countries, especially Tanzania and Ethiopia, but with no appreciable success so far."

Egypt is the second-largest economy in Africa, and the bilateral volume of trade with Russia has more than doubled since 2021; in 2025, according to Russia's Federal Customs Service, it was $10.5 billion (€9.4 billion). Consignments of Russian grain are the main drivers, followed by products of the metal industry. Egypt's exports to Russia are primarily fruit and vegetables.

There are investment projects, too. Russia is building a big nuclear power plant in the Egyptian region of El-Dabaa on the Mediterranean coast. Construction is being financed by a Russian loan of 25 billion US dollars, which covers around 85% of the costs.

Egypt is one of the few African countries with which Russia enjoys stable business relationships, as well as having extensive experience of cooperation, says Nikita Smagin, an expert on Russian policy in the Middle East. "In the long term, Egypt could become Moscow's gateway to Africa and to other markets," he says. "But Cairo is pursuing its own interests. It would be too optimistic to hope that Egypt is lending its support purely out of political solidarity."

According to the Russian customs service, around 39% of Russian–African trade in 2025 was with Egypt, and total sales between Russia and all 54 countries of the African continent came to around 27 billion US dollars. Africa's share of Russia's foreign trade is therefore very small (3.9% in 2025), and not at all commensurate with the attention Moscow is devoting to its relations with African countries.

Russia is not a significant trading partner for Africa, either. The most important partner for African countries is the European Union. In 2025, the volume of trade with the EU came to around 385 billion US dollars. African countries' statistics also show that other partners were well ahead of Russia. The volume of trade with China was in excess of 348 billion US dollars in 2025; with the United States it was almost 105 billion, and 103 billion with India.

Fidel Owusu, a Ghanaian expert with Geopolitical Intelligence Services (GIS) in Liechtenstein, comments that Russia's economic presence in Africa has not been as significant as that of China, the United States, India, or other traditional powers like France and Britain. "If you look at the volume of trade and the kind of investment," he says, "in recent times, some middle powers such as Turkey and the UAW are doing far better than Russia."

Beverly Ochieng, a senior analyst with Control Risks, a global risk and strategic intelligence consultancy in Senegal, observes: "Western countries continue to dominate in strategically important areas such as raw material extraction, finance, and the energy sector, even if their political presence in the region is declining." According to her, "Russia will compete more intensively for access to critical mineral resources and energy projects. We see this with lithium projects in Mali as well as with nuclear power initiatives across the continent."

Russia's presence in Africa is more obvious in the military sector than in the fields of trade and investment. Starting with the arrival of the Wagner Group, Russian mercenaries have been supporting African regimes, particularly those of the unstable countries in the Sahel region. In exchange, their associated subsidiaries are granted access to raw materials. Following the death of the Wagner Group leader, Yevgeny Prigozhin, most of these operations were taken over by the Africa Corps, a paramilitary group set up and controlled by Russia's defense ministry.

According to the Congressional Research Service, the think tank of the US Congress, the largest Russian military contingents, each comprising several thousand men, are in the Central African Republic, Mali, and Libya. The Africa Corps is also keen to extend its presence in Burkina Faso and Niger. Russian mercenaries have also been spotted in Equatorial Guinea.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Irina Filatova from the University of Cape Town stresses that there are several reasons why it's important for Russia to maintain a military presence in Africa. "The countries have sizeable deposits of minerals such as gold and uranium. Through them, it's possible to exert influence over Europe's southern borders, including in matters of migration and regional security. With regard to Libya, the country is an important logistical hub for connections with the Sahel and central Africa. Goods can easily be supplied via Libya to countries without access to the sea," Filatova says.

Ultimately, Russia is still one of the biggest suppliers of arms to African countries, even though Russian exports have fallen over the course of the war in Ukraine. The Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) estimates Moscow's share of the African market for the years 2021–2025 at 15%, which puts it in third place behind the United States (19%) and China (17%). Between 2020 and 2024, its share was even higher: It was in first place with 21%, followed by China with 18%, and the US with 16%.

Ivan Klyszcz from the ICDS says that while Russia is not a significant economic partner for Africa, the fact that it supplies food and fertilizer and has a military presence in some countries means that Moscow's influence in Africa is far greater than is suggested by the volume of trade and investment alone.

"I believe Russia sees the diplomatic weight of Africa," says Fidel Owusu. "When I talk of diplomatic weight, I mean numbers – the continent has the largest number of countries. Russia wants that kind of support in the UN General Assembly whenever votes are cast. In recent times it has done better than in earlier votes."

In recent years, Russia has been positioning itself on the international stage as representing the interests of the Global South.

"We want to work with Africa, we are working with Africa and we will continue to do so. But our aim is not, as it was for the colonial powers, to make money or steal something from Africa, but to develop together," Russian president Vladimir Putin said recently at a conference of the Moscow-based Valdai Discussion Club.

References to the colonial past appeal to some countries but not others, says Irina Filatova. "Africa is not a country, it's a continent. There are differences in the perception of Russia, as well as in the way Russia positions itself. Also, the views of the political elites are often substantially different from those of ordinary citizens. In South Africa, for instance, the Russian narrative is received very positively. An anti-colonial agenda is also popular in other countries, but it isn't necessarily associated with Russia."

Antonio Cascais contributed to this report. It was originally written in Russian.

#829. Bob Dylan, 85, Meets With Pope Leo XIV in Rare Public Appearance

Bob Dylan stepped out for a meeting with Pope Leo XIV on Nov. 4, marking a rare public appearance for the 85-year-old musician.

All along the watchtower, eyes were on the Vatican as Pope Leo XIV (born Robert Francis Prevost) crossed paths with Bob Dylan (born Robert Allen Zimmerman).

After all, Dylan has long been known for knock, knock, knockin’ on Heaven’s door, and this time the way opened up for a private meeting between the head of the Catholic church and the celebrated musician on Nov. 4.

For the occasion, Dylan and Pope Leo’s outfits painted a humorously opposite picture. Where Pope Leo, 71, was a vision in white in a classic cassock, Dylan was dressed in black almost entirely from head to toe, including a jacket he wore with the hood up during the meeting.

As for what exactly the singer and the pontiff pontificated about, Vatican News reported only that the pair swapped greetings and “a few lighthearted exchanges” during the “brief” meeting. The Pope reportedly gave Dylan a rosary, while the singer gave the Catholic leader a copy of his autobiography, Chronicles: Volume One.

Meanwhile, Vatican official Rev. Antonio Spadaro—who helped organize the rendezvous—shared what it was like to witness the meeting.

“It was hard not to feel the emotion of being part of an encounter that had a real sense of history about it,” Spadaro wrote on social media, “with the feeling that, at every step through the Apostolic Palace, absolutely anything could happen!”

But in a world where anything can, in fact, happen, this particular meeting seemed somewhat preordained, with Leo have previously proven his Dylan fandom.

Back in July, the Pope quoted Dylan’s work in Disarmed and Disarming: Peace is a Gift, a book published by the Vatican Publishing House. In the book’s preface, the Pope cited Dylan’s 1963 nuclear protest song “Go Away You Bomb.”

Specifically, Leo recalled the line, “I hate you cause yer man-made and man-owned, an’ man-handled.”

The American-born Leo, however, is not the first Pope into whose orbit the wind has blown Dylan, 85.

In fact, back in 1997, the singer-songwriter performed for Pope John Paul II at the 23rd National Eucharistic Congress in Bologna, Italy.

John Paul, too, looked to Dylan’s lyrics to inspire, quoting from his song “Blowin’ in the Wind” in an address to the crowd of 30,000 that was at the event.

“You ask me, ‘How many roads must a man walk down / before you can call him a man?’” the Pope asked, adding, “Only one. There is only one road for man, and that is the road of Jesus Christ.”

#827. Arsenal have everything they need to repeat as Premier League champions | Jonathan Wilson

Sunday’s win at Liverpool showed the Gunners are deeper, more experienced, and are playing against a weaker class of contenders than last season

Arsenal are three points clear at the top of the Premier League table. But given the team in second are Manchester City, who are likely to be facing at the very least a major points deduction, perhaps more significant is that they are five clear of Brighton in third. The season of domination that many anticipated from the champions appears to be coming to pass.

Liverpool challenged them on Sunday. There was a 20-minute spell before half-time when they swarmed all over Arsenal, and Anfield felt at least like it did in the golden years of Jürgen Klopp, when it buzzed with an energy that could overwhelm visitors. But Arsenal got through that, reset at half-time, and navigated the second half with relative comfort. For the second league game running, they denied Liverpool a shot on target.

If there is a lesson, it is that Liverpool, like Brighton, demonstrated that a very aggressive press can unsettle Arsenal. But then, a very aggressive press can unsettle anybody. In Arsenal’s loss at Brighton, Pascal Gross and Charalampos Kostoulas took difficult opportunities; at Anfield Liverpool were denied what should surely have been a penalty when Jurriën Timber tugged Alexander Isak’s shirt – another bad moment for VAR, in that the no-call essentially mandated players to go down and highlight contact. Later, Alexis Mac Allister put a free header over. That was the difference, and this Arsenal team will not give opponents many chances. They are good at closing games out. Ezri Konsa in particular was outstanding on Sunday.

They also have a strong bench. The policy has been to make the squad deeper rather than adding the very highest quality – which is why the links with Vinícius Júnior over the summer were so unexpected. That has frustrated some, but it has been successful. Arsenal on Sunday could bring on Myles Lewis-Skelly, Piero Hincapié, Viktor Gyökeres and Mikel Merino to protect their lead with very little diminution of quality. But it’s not just on a man-to-man level that Liverpool’s options suffer by comparison; their changes upset the balance. They never really had control of the game once Dominik Szoboszlai had come on for Trey Nyoni.

It’s been a recurring feature of this season that Arsenal turn half-time draws into full-time wins – it’s already happened seven times. Winning individual games, though, is only part of it; a deeper squad means there can be more rotation, which should help prevent fatigue as the season goes on, as well as providing additional cover when injuries do occur. That said, their depth was not sufficient to get them past Fleetwood in the Carabao Cup last week, although they will face few games in conditions as challenging as those on the Lancashire coast.

There are still three-quarters of the season to go, and Arsenal were in a similarly commanding position at this stage last season, four points clear of second-placed Bournemouth after nine games. The expectation then was for a procession that didn’t materialise and looked, amid a spring wobble, to have gone awry. Then as now the feeling was not merely that Arsenal were very good, but that none of their rivals looked especially threatening.

But this season they have the memory of winning the title; the insecurity of three successive second-place finishes should be lessened. There is a resilience to them that has already brought a first win at Anfield since 2012 and a victory at Nottingham Forest after successive goalless draws at the City Ground. They’re picking up points at grounds where they’ve stumbled.

Last season, City were more resilient than had been anticipated. It may be a different story this time, and not just because of the potential for a savage points deduction. After seven straight wins they have lost successive league games to Aston Villa and Brighton, but the vulnerabilities that have been exposed had been apparent earlier in the season: a high defensive line that can be exploited. Liverpool are starting to coalesce under Andoni Iraola but they haven’t clicked quite yet and are, anyway, nine points adrift. Chelsea are a point better off but still a work in progress. Brighton have probably been the best other side, but they don’t have the depth to be considered a title challenger.

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

Sunday made clear what was already widely suspected: Arsenal are the best team in the league by some margin. It’s not just their depth, their cohesion and the wide variety of situations from which they can score goals, it’s that they now have belief and are picking up points at places where they have often failed in the past. And if they do build up a substantial lead by Easter, that could be hugely beneficial to their European challenge, which remains the one unconquered frontier.

#825. EU's 'Made in Europe' push unnerves global auto suppliers

In shielding Europe's carmakers from Chinese rivals, the EU risks hurting close partners from Turkey and Morocco to Japan and South Korea. Billions in trade and hundreds of thousands of European jobs are at stake.

It is meant to save Europe's auto industry from China's unfair trade practices. The European Union's Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), proposed in March, seeks to upgrade European car factories and only subsidize vehicles produced in Europe.

Yet, the EU's "Made in Europe" plan is causing deep concern among other allied carmaking nations — such as Turkey, Morocco, Japan and South Korea — all of them deeply embedded in European supply chains.

After months of deadlock over the IAA's potential impact on their own vehicle production, Germany and France earlier this month reached a key compromise that would allow suppliers from non-EU members like the United Kingdom and Norway to qualify for "European origin" status.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Other key players in the automotive sector, however, will be excluded — including Turkey, which has enjoyed seamless access to the EU market since the mid-1990s.

While the proposals still face major legislative hurdles in Brussels before becoming law, Ayhan Zeytinoglu, chairman of the Economic Development Foundation (IKV), thinks the Franco-German framework could be devastating for Turkey's auto sector.

"73% of Turkey’s total automotive exports go to the EU," Zeytinoglu told DW. "If we encounter a 'Made in Europe' barrier in the EU market, this will cause great damage to our trade with the EU and to our exports."

Excluding Turkey would also harm European automaking rather than strengthen competitiveness against China, he added.

Turkey's auto exporters association OIB calculated that the country's automotive exports to the EU totaled $30.1 billion (€26.8 billion) last year.

The IAA requires that 70% of the total value of a vehicle's components — excluding the battery — should be made in Europe.

However, the initial proposal only applies to battery-electric vehicles (EVs), plug-in hybrids and fuel-cell models, which last year made up just 27% of all new EU car registrations.

Tommaso Pardi, director of the international automotive research network GERPISA and a senior researcher at the French National Center for Scientific Research (CNRS), notes that the 70% target is remarkably generous.

"If you take an average European-made electric car and take away the battery, you would find that around 83% [of parts] come from Europe," Pardi told DW.

Under the revised German-French plan, some self-charging hybrids and petrol and diesel vehicles could still be sold after 2035 and would also be affected by the "Made in Europe" rules.

These cars contain a much lower proportion of European parts. Most of Turkey's nearly 800,000 vehicle exports to the EU last year would fall under this much larger umbrella.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Another key reason for excluding Turkey is that Chinese automakers are expanding their presence there, hoping to gain back-door access to the EU market, but face major roadblocks.

They include SWM Motors, whose factory in the northwestern city of Eskisehir closed within a year because the cars produced didn't meet EU safety standards.

BYD's plans to open a $1 billion plant in Manisa — a large industrial hub near the Aegean coast — have been put on hold.

Morocco, meanwhile, has received Chinese investments worth more than €10 billion ($11 billion) since the COVID-19 pandemic, according to consultancy AlixPartners, much of it in batteries and auto parts.

For France, the North African nation plays a similar role to China for Germany's auto sector — a low-cost production hub that helps French carmakers stay competitive. Budget-friendly French models would likely become more expensive if Morocco were excluded.

Japanese carmakers, which build several of their models in European factories, could also lose out. Cars imported from Japan would not qualify for EU subsidies, while models built in France, Portugal and Eastern Europe would benefit only if enough of their parts come from Europe.

South Korean automakers, meanwhile, could also be hurt. Hyundai and Kia build cars in the Czech Republic and Slovakia, but also ship models from Asia, which would not qualify. Korean battery plants in Poland and Hungary, however, would count as European.

Pardi notes how European car giants are actively lobbying to water down the IAA to protect their high profit margins.

"They want to limit the IAA to retain the biggest scope to still source from abroad, particularly from China," he said.

EU-based automakers warn that higher parts costs would put them at an even bigger disadvantage against Chinese rivals, while European battery supply is unlikely to meet demand anytime soon.

Ankara is also lobbying Brussels to be included in the "Made in Europe" program, while automakers are seeking a compromise that would allow Turkey to join at a later stage.

Pardi said this would be "only for European companies that are based there [Turkey and Morocco] ... while excluding all recent investments involving Chinese capital [in those countries]."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

European auto-parts suppliers are, however, on the opposite side of the argument, calling for further strengthening of IAA. They warn that up to 650,000 auto jobs in the region could be lost by 2035 without better protection for their members.

"A lost industrial job is very hard to win back, and the damage reaches well beyond large suppliers," Benjamin Krieger, Secretary General of the European Association of Automotive Suppliers (CLEPA), told DW.

Krieger thinks the IAA helps European industry to level the playing field against unfair competition from China, adding: "We must stop the bleeding."

With broad public support for measures that ensure that EU public funding "benefits value creation in Europe," CLEPA's Krieger thinks allies like Turkey, Morocco, South Korea and Japan may not lose out if they meet the EU's criteria.

"The EU should offer access to the IAA through an opt-in mechanism with objective criteria: regulatory alignment, social and environmental standards, no market distortion, respect for the rule of law and reciprocity, backed by anti-circumvention measures. Partners that meet them are welcome," he said.

#824. Revisiting the Superclásico: a story of death, violence, colour and family

Attending Boca v River in the week I turned 60 made me recall a lifetime of experiences at the fixture

Ever since the Observer Sport Monthly published a list of 50 sporting things you must do before you die with Watch Boca Juniors Play River Plate in Buenos Aires at No 1 in 2004, the biggest super derby in Argentina has been firmly positioned in the global imagination; its reputation for colour, passion and uncontainable emotion acquiring an almost glamorous sheen. The thump and thud of the coordinated chants, the shiny ticker-tape amid flare smoke matching the teams’ strips, the bounce of the concrete as tens of thousands jump in unison, mounted police surrounding the stadium, avalanche stoppers set alight, rockets aimed at players; blood and fire.

Things have changed, though, and Sunday at La Bombonera (Boca’s stadium known as the Chocolate Box) was quite a different spectacle. Since 2013 football matches in Argentina have been played without visiting fans, so for starters the colour palette has been greatly reduced. The absence of the opposing tribe has been welcomed by many, making the experience of going to a football match more family-friendly and increasing ticket availability for club members.

As we shared a choripán in a corner grill before the game, the Argentinian journalist Ezequiel Fernández Moores recalls the first Superclásico without away fans, at the Monumental in 2013. As Boca’s Emmanuel Gigliotti scored to give the away team the lead, in the press area Moores heard the beginning “G” of someone ready to shout the goal with glee, suddenly realising “non-home joy had to be repressed”.

Over the years the absence of away fans has been mirrored in an absence of away press. Now the journalists sit at their desks along the same height as the middle tier of the traditional home end, where the heart of the hardcore organised gang known as La Doce leads the rhythm section, creating a sense of continuum, with hacks clad in Boca strips cursing and cheering along with the crowd.

Rain had been forecast for Sunday so Boca distributed blue and yellow umbrellas which opened in sync and matched the colour of the smoke from the fireworks organised by the club.

The pyrotechnics used to be smuggled in by La Doce, who would also orchestrate the release of blue and golden balloons at the exact time the players emerged from the tunnel. When I went to pick up my accreditation, the head press officer announced to no one in particular that this “Señora” (meaning me) had once interviewed José Barritta. A young man holding a newborn baby and a couple of kids who looked barely out of school just stared. “The day of the Ambush,” I stated by way of explanation.

Barritta was the infamous leader of La Doce decades ago and in 1994 I did indeed spend the afternoon with him to write a colour piece about the Superclásico from the “middle tray” (the terraces are tiered in three balconies and the middle one is the centre of operations). It was an afternoon that would end in tragedy with two River Plate fans shot dead after the game. Disgustingly, graffiti emerged nearby soon afterwards reading “River 2 Boca 2”, equating two young lives to the two goals River had scored against Boca securing their victory.

My feature was shelved and instead I became a witness to the fact that Barritta had not been involved, my work published in a human rights journal, and my interest in football-related violence swiftly losing the wide-eyed fascination.

Death at the Superclásico was not something new, even then. In 1968, 71 fans – mostly Boca – were crushed when one of the exit gates for away supporters didn’t fully open. Known as the incident of Puerta 12, much of what actually happened remains unknown, but El Gráfico reported the following year’s game saw members of both Boca and River fans chant together against the police. In those days both gangs were friendly, with then-Boca gang leader Quique, who ran a grill opposite the stadium, buying meat from River gang leader “El Tano Mingo”, who was a butcher. They would often join forces and combat against other club gangs well into the mid-1970s when the leaderships changed. Barritta took the helm of La Doce in 1981, by which time the rupture was total.

In 2018 Boca and River met in the Libertadores final, South America’s version of the Champions League, and the Argentina president, Mauricio Macri, thought it might be fun to show the world what a colourful spectacle the Superclásico might be, so away fans were allowed back to the stadium in a one-off experiment. After the Boca bus was attacked with stones and crowd control fell apart around the inner ring surrounding the River stadium, fans were kept under strict orders to remain in place for close to five hours while the powers that be discussed options. The match was cancelled and outrageously moved to Madrid, where one could argue the soul of the Superclásico has remained, if it hadn’t been sucked out already.

Sunday’s game was not a fixture of the calibre of a Libertadores final. In fact, the strangeness of the current system in Argentina means it was almost inconsequential for either cup or league, although a total points system known as the Argentina Table has implied that Boca’s underwhelming 1-0 victory against a River side down to nine men by the end means Boca have a place in next year’s Libertadores.

“I’ve seen better Superclásicos,” said the radio commentator Victor Hugo Morales in his tiny cabin at the stadium. He was commemorating 60 years to the day of his very first radio commentary, back in Uruguay in 1966. I went along to exchange greetings, as I was commemorating 60 years to the day of being alive. “But I’ve also seen worse,” he added.

That must be debatable, though I’ve probably not seen as many as him. The derby doesn’t always offer the best football, often too embroiled in the hype and the media frenzy surrounding it, and the massive banners and flags obscuring the view for most of the pitch. I started going to the Bombonera with my cousins as a teenager, and the most poignant memory of the fixture was taking my 10-year-old brother along without telling my dad. In those days, women and children got in for free. On Sunday, tickets were going for half a million pesos (£240).

I remember grabbing the little boy by the waist of his trousers as I saw him flying above a sea of sweaty men, as I heard someone shout: “Careful you lot, there’s a ‘Señora’ here!” I was 20. I felt perfectly safe, but I couldn’t convey that to my furious father, who I don’t think I’d ever seen so angry, before or since.

Years later, when TV rights took possession of the industry and football became pay-per-view, my dad was one of the early adopters of a codified system which enabled live watching. I suggested our dear family friend Klaus, a River fan, desperate to watch the Superclásico, join my brothers and cousins atDad’s. Klaus didn’t reveal his allegiance and sat quietly in grief while the assorted Boca fiends jumped about in joy when they won. The anecdote is remembered fondly to this day in my family but for him it was a particularly unpleasant experience.

Maybe new generations will be better at bridging the cultural crack. Streamer Davo, the face of new sports media, was nonchalant before the game. “Don’t give me all this Superclásico nonsense. For me, nothing changes if River beats us this game. I’m focused on the Argentina Cup, on the South American final … this is just another match.”

Also seemingly oblivious to the hyped-up frenzied vitriol, my own son had suggested we go to the game together. He, a River fan, however, could not in any realistic sense attend. I’d love to go to a Superclásico with my son, neither one of us banned by the other’s tribe. Maybe one day.

#823. 14 Gifts the New York City Girl in Your Life Will Actually Want

Whether she’s commuting, exploring, or getting ready for a night out, these thoughtful picks fit right into her busy city life.

Whether you also live in the city or you have a long-distance bestie, gift shopping for the New York City girl in your life can feel impossible. They probably have it all, and if they don’t, they live in the best place to get it in person. Unless you get a FaceTime haul every time they shop, you probably have a slim chance to get the perfect gift for them.

It can be hard to be tapped into the NYC lifestyle enough to know what they want (before they even know they want it). Luckily, I got you. While I wasn’t born and raised in New York, I have been living here for five years now. And as a shopping writer, I’ve tried plenty of products throughout the year to be able to tell you what the average NYC girl would want to get under the tree this year.

When in doubt, opt for gifts that have a sleek city vibe, are practical for on-the-go, and actually work. We recommend starting with a chic pouch (or tin can) that you can customize with their name, and filling it with luxury skincare, hair, makeup, and fragrance minis. Then, choose a good-quality item based on their vibe—whether it’s a wool coat, a screenless digital camera, or a shoulder bag.

So, keep scrolling to shop for the best gifts for the NYC girl in your life, according to this NYC writer.

Available in new limited-edition holiday shades, this gorgeous lip gloss serum is infused with hyaluronic acid, squalane, and castor oil to leave your lips soft, shiny, and lightly tinted. Plus, it comes in a convenient (and chic) tin that fits in every mini bag you need while you’re out in the city.

Looking for custom embroidery? Abbode is an iconic spot in SoHo to get just that. There are so many options to choose from, but my heart was captured by this sleek and stylish croc pouch that you can customize with their signature or a phrase and decorate with a cute icon. Imagine gifting them this with lots of chic minis inside? Obsessed.

Created by celebrity makeup artist Mary Phillips, the m.ph brand is that line in Sephora everyone wishes they had in their collection. With its sleek packaging and amazing formulas, it’s practically made for the city girl. If you don’t have their specific shade for the new foundation, we recommend the viral underpainting palette that started it all.

Whether your NYC bestie loves to host or needs a cheeky drink before bed, these martini glasses are perfect for their home with their custom name engraved in a variety of font options.

Looking for a film-type camera without the hassle of going somewhere to develop it, but still want to have an air of mystery of how the photos turned out? The Camp Snap screenless digital camera is exactly that. It’s lightweight enough to throw in your bag, and has four film-style modes with a built-in memory that’s incredibly fun to play around.

Outside In’s flagship store recently opened in the LES, with a full coffee bar, lovely garden backyard, a fragrance gallery, a makeup section, and a Nature of Things spa-like section. If you’re looking to gift something from this brand, I recommend the mascara, with its skinny “cig-like” and luxe silver packaging and formula full of tubing technology, shea butter, vegan waxes, and more.

This winter, you don’t have to put away all of your ballet flats. Legwarmers will be all over the city this season, so get these faux fur ones from Urban Outfitters that feature a chic neutral colorway and fuzzy texture.

Whether they’re waiting for their next train underground or touching up in the Uber, every city girl needs a luxe hairbrush (or two) while they’re on the go. La Bonne Brosse is simply that brand. This set includes a small version of their iconic boar bristle brush and a wide-tooth comb in a matching lovely pink colorway.

In my NYC closet, there can never be too many sneakers—especially when they’re a trendy chocolate shade, low-profile, and extremely comfortable for walking around for hours. Extra points if they’re a K-Pop (and Blackpink) fan, because these new Puma x Rosé sneakers are a perfect gift.

You can also never have too many bags! This Kate Spade shoulder bag is delicate and practical for city living (and absolutely gorgeous in person), with its icy lavender shade, suede texture, silver hardware, 3D flower details, and adjustable shoulder strap.

Every NYC girl needs a good cleansing routine for when she gets home after a whole day out in the city. Make that routine better with this gift set that includes these bestselling ELEMIS cleansing balms and soft cleansing cuffs.

Every city girl needs a good facial, and this skincare device gives the most relaxing one right at home. Mount Lai’s Gua Sha device features a 660nm red LED light, up to 113F degree heat therapy, and white jade rollers that’ll leave your skin smooth and sculpted.

Your bestie might have a whole fragrance collection, but does she have luxury scents in chic mini sizes? Not only are they adorable, but they’re also so handy for all on-the-go it girls. This fragrance set from Maison Francis Kurkdjian features five of the brand’s top-rated scents in small glass vials.

When it comes to gifting coats and sweaters to your friend who lives in New York, opt for one that has 100% (or a majority) natural fibers that’ll actually keep them warm this season. This Madewell coat is 100% wool and features a relaxed fit, a convertible funnel-neck collar, dolman sleeves, and cozy welt pockets.

Looking for more gifts? Shop the best purses and bags to gift this holiday season!

#821. Asian Cup postponement leaves Socceroos, FA and coach Tony Popovic at crossroads | Joey Lynch

The most immediate question thrown up by the delay of the tournament in Saudi Arabia is what it now means for Popovic

Confirmation that the Asian Cup has been postponed until December 2027 would have caught few by surprise. But the timing of Tuesday’s announcement might have, given it came well ahead of the late November timeframe hinted at by the AFC. Yet with Houthi attacks continuing across Saudi Arabia, it felt inevitable the tournament would be deferred.

However foreseeable though, it has left the Socceroos, their coach Tony Popovic and Football Australia at a crossroads.

It is a major tournament the Socceroos harboured hopes of winning. Japan would have been considered favourites; the Samurai Blue, despite having been underachievers since winning in 2011, have earned that mantle. But, despite back-to-back quarter-final exits, Australia are also acknowledged as a continental heavyweight by their peers, coming off a World Cup in which they were one of only two Asian sides to progress to the knockout stages. And with rivals such as Qatar, South Korea and Iran all aging and/or experiencing significant upheaval, the regional picture suggested they should have challenged in January.

Popovic would have been able to take to Saudi Arabia a side brimming with young talent and boasting an enviable combination of consistent improvement and valuable World Cup experience. They would have been building on an October window in which they twice met Brazil and a pair of ideal preparatory games against the 2023 Asian Cup finalists, Qatar and Jordan, in November.

Even with fitness concerns hovering over Mohamed Touré and Jordy Bos, the talent and momentum was there for the Socceroos to win a second Asian crown.

Nonetheless, there are silver linings. The tournament may benefit from a 12-month delay, as it will feel less like a post-World Cup afterthought. The postponement could also allow the Socceroos to further evolve and become even better by Christmas next year.

Another 11 months means further development, both for the Socceroos as a collective and for individuals such as Nestory Irankunda, Paul Okon-Engstler, Alessandro Circati and Lucas Herrington. Following their recent high-profile moves to some of Europe’s biggest clubs and leagues, that progression could be significant. It also allows for injured players such as Bos, Touré and Lewis Miller time to recover, while other youngsters yet to establish themselves get more time to impress.

In this scenario, the hope is that a bird in the hand isn’t worth two in the bush – that more injuries don’t strike and that veterans such as Jackson Irvine and Aziz Behich maintain their current form.

But the more immediate question arising from the announcement is what it means for Popovic. The November window is now ostensibly the 53-year-old’s last as Socceroos coach; the contract extension he signed ahead of the World Cup, which was supposed to take him through this tournament, concludes on a definitive date rather than a nebulous “post Asian Cup” marker.

Popovic and Football Australia face a challenge neither would have expected when they hammered out – at the coach’s insistence – a deal that only took him through to the end of the continental showpiece. A similar scenario confronts Graham Arnold with Iraq, while Japan have already signalled that Hajime Moriyasu will be replaced by Go Oiwa.

Sign up for expert analysis from Jonathan Wilson as well as a rundown of Australians playing in the major leagues

Is it now simply a matter of extending Popovic’s deal through to 21 January 2028? Given the federation offered him that longer-term deal, and executives such as Heather Garriock and Martin Kugeler have never been anything but effusive in their praise, it’s almost certain Popovic would be able to if he wants. But does he?

He would have had his reasons for not wanting to be locked into a longer-term deal. And as a football-obsessed workhorse, it’s entirely possible he’d have ambitions to return to the grind of club football. His stock is high after leading the Socceroos to the World Cup’s knockout stages, and further bolstered by a window where his side performed well against Brazil and he drew praise from Carlo Ancelotti. If he wants a new challenge, he has earned one.

But what if he stays, only to depart after another 12 months? Kevin Muscat has always appeared to be an obvious successor, especially given he’ll be a free agent after the imminent conclusion of the Chinese Super League. And if Popovic does opt to depart, he should be offered the job. But would he – or another preferred candidate – be willing to wait a year, especially with World Cup qualification will still beginning in September? Does Football Australia risk being left to scramble come 2028 if they don’t play their cards right?

Just like seemingly everything else in Australian football, the postponement of the Asian Cup presents as both a potential opportunity and a curse.

#820. Kim Kardashian Reveals She Eats "Prop Food" on All's Fair Set

Kim Kardashian admitted she often eats the prop food on the set of Hulu's All's Fair, costarring Sarah Paulson, Glenn Close, Niecy Nash-Betts, Teyana Taylor and Naomi Watts.

For Kim Kardashian, all's fair on the set of All's Fair.

That's why she has no problem eating prop food while filming scenes with costars Sarah Paulson, Niecy Nash-Betts, Naomi Watts, Glenn Close and Teyana Taylor for their Hulu legal drama.

"It's real food and I eat it the whole time," Kardashian said during the cast's Nov. 4 appearance on Good Morning America. "I'll be walking by after they cut and I'm like, 'Can I take a plate of that pie with me?'"

And her castmates have objections to her unusual snacking habit. As Nash-Betts quipped, "Do not let that tiny body fool you: She eats everything."

"I said, 'This is prop food! Why are you eating this?'" she continued with a laugh. "This is the greediest woman I've ever met in my life."

But there's a reason why Kardashian's costars have dismissed prop food.

"We don't want to eat it all day," Paulson explained, with Watts adding, "It's a thing called continuity. If you eat it in the scene, you have to keep doing it."

However, their testimonies haven't swayed Kardashian one bit.

"Because I'm new to this, they tried to tell me, 'Hey, continuity. Pace yourself. Eat a grape or half a grape because you're gonna have to do that the same time 50 times,'" the 46-year-old shared. "By the end, I am like, 'What did I get myself into?' But I love it."

In fact, the Keeping Up With the Kardashians alum has even recreated some of her own snacks with Rice Krispies off set. As she put it, "Last night in my room, I made Rice Krispie treats because I wanted all the girls to try them."

And while the jury's still out on Kardashian as a cook, her costars have been thoroughly impressed by her acting skills.

"Her ability to remember her lines, she's so good with that," Taylor raved to E! News last year. "She'll keep reading it over and over and over again. It's dope to see."

Added Close, "She's a very sweet woman, she does her homework, she has great people around her, which says a lot."

To find out what other stars are snacking on these days, read on...

"Fruit and raw nuts. Recently I've made an effort to keep lost of fresh products and nuts on hand for snacking in-between meals."

"I am snacking so much while I've been at home! I think it's because I'm home and near my fridge all day. I slice up an apple and it fills me up between meals. I love the satisfying crunch and so do my kids."

"My go-to snack is canned oysters. I know that might sound weird, but I am absolutely obsessed with canned oysters. They are such a good source of protein, magnesium and vitamin C. They are so tasty and always fill me up. I eat them straight out of the can, but sometimes if I want some extra carbs, I'll eat them with crackers and the crunch of the cracker with the soft oyster is so good!"

"Carrots and hummus is always a fave with a handful of raw almonds and/or cashews."

"I always have a cup of fruit near me, usually with grapes or berries. For drinks, I like homemade green juice. I mix in BODYARMOR Lyte, Coconut for some sweetness and flavor without having to worry about sugar."

"Handfuls of roasted, unsalted almonds, a slice of sourdough bread with cashew butter and sliced bananas, a smoothie (mine usually have whole milk Greek yogurt, ice, a handful of spinach, some pineapple, whatever milk I have (right now it is Forager Coconut Cashew Oat), a banana, half an avocado, two dates, a dash of cinnamon (and sometimes a scoop of nut butter)."

"Hot Cheetos and fruit with tajin and lemon, yummy!"

"Fruit! I can't think of a more perfect food."

"Cheese and crackers with lots of cheese."

"Apples and peanut butter but not just your average apples and peanut butter, folks. There is a science to this special snack. First, they have to be honeycrisp apples, cut very thin. Then you get your peanut butter, melt it, add some honey and stir all the deliciousness together! This creates almost like a caramel consistency. You don't use nearly as much peanut butter and you avoid getting it on your thumb every time you dip. Brilliant, I know!"

#819. Mainoo and Lacey raise the spirits but systemic change still required at Manchester United | Nick Ames

There were protests at Old Trafford and even though two academy products stood out, Michael Carrick’s future is far from safe

Green and yellow balloons bobbed around the Stretford End. Tennis balls rained down on the pitch in protest at the chronic, enduringly cinematic decline presided over by Manchester United’s ownership. Then came a reminder of the humble football’s extraordinary power to bend history, minds and wills. United’s players departed victorious having somehow won the game within the game, separating themselves from the fog of unhappy context swirling on all sides and turning the second half into its own soaring, ripping story for the ages.

Will it be enough to save Michael Carrick, who was once again serenaded when minds wandered from the joint scourges of the Glazer family and Jim Ratcliffe? If Aston Villa defend a shade more competently than Roma on Sunday then perhaps not. United have led their supporters, remarkable in their tenor of backing for players and head coach here, up more than enough false peaks over the past 13 years. Arguably, that is one reason for Carrick being given the job on a permanent basis.

Until United are equipped to repeat their second 45 minutes on a weekly basis, which requires systemic change in departments far outside the technical area, even if Carrick’s head will surely be first on the block, nobody is likely to deliver them from ongoing psychodrama. History may tell that his heavily maligned players were fruitlessly raging against the dying of the light in blowing Roma out of the water. But their achievement here was worth savouring for its discrete brilliance and, perhaps, the wholesome powers that ultimately wrought it.

Kobbie Mainoo had been introduced as “Manchester born and bred”, to obligatory cheers, when the teams were read out. Any emotional heartstring is worth plucking on at the moment but there was something grounding about seeing the midfielder, largely injured over the past month and an onlooker while his colleagues’ fortunes spiralled, return to the starting XI. Mainoo was far from alone in enduring a tentative, twitchy, flustered first half but was caught flat-footed when Marten de Roon mugged him near halfway, setting in train the move that exposed an execrably organised backline for Matías Soulé’s opener.

At 2-0, another crossfield ball from the left having triggered United’s defence into recidivism, Mainoo attempted to raise spirits by surging through the middle on his own and spraying the ball right under pressure. There was no more nourishing gruel on offer than this; the only nagging glimmer of possibility was that Roma, for all their broad control, did not look like the kind of side that would withstand any gale that came their way.

When Carlos Baleba, eye-catching in phases but loose in possession, pulled up with Bryan Mbeumo ready for a tap-in, the notes of misery deepened. But the subsequent introduction of Youri Tielemans, in his element against opponents whose intensity was evidently sagging, created angles and spaces that had previously seemed figments of the mind. United were fortunate when Bruno Fernandes converted his soft, twice-taken penalty; they were presented with parity when Leonardo Balerdi’s air-kick afforded Matheus Cunha a chance he could barely miss. The die, though, had long been cast through their waves of slick, insistent pressure.

So it fell for Mainoo and another academy product, Shea Lacey, to tee up the coup de grace. Lacey hails from Liverpool but there is no need to whisper that: his credentials since childhood have firmly passed muster. While Lisandro Martínez was lightly booed on to the pitch in the 75th minute, Lacey arrived with him to raptures. How poetic it was that Mainoo, speeding up an attack before quickly shifting the ball right, and the mesmerising Lacey, should complete the revival.

Lacey’s jink inside and left-footed pass whipped into Cunha were genuinely breathtaking. So was the finish and so, too, the reaction. Few do it quite like an Old Trafford crowd on a European night. This is still a citadel like no other, even if its strains nowadays alternate between dubbing Mainoo unplayable and impolitely requesting the Glazers to make haste back across the Atlantic.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

The contradictions fizzed everywhere on this thick, still night. Earlier on Wednesday Carrick will doubtless have been spared the news that sacking season had already visited the Ineos football empire. At this point Jim Ratcliffe’s sporting citadels are more akin to a line of Dickensian rubbish heaps, their proprietor a modern-day golden dustman, and the plug had been pulled on Luka Elsner and United’s hapless junior sibling, Lausanne Sport. They are bottom of the Swiss top flight and results, a club statement explained, had been the determining factor in the manager’s demise.

They have not exactly helped Carrick either. Mainoo had claimed in a transactionally toned pre-match press conference that United could be “one win away” from changing the shape and scope of their season. In reality all that can be guaranteed about whatever occurs next is the sheer theatre of it. Of course it is Unai Emery, discussion whose suitability or otherwise for any United vacancy has brought surprising ramifications, who walks into this perplexing cocktail of loathing and unconditional support this weekend. Carrick will need the football to perform him a few more favours yet.

#818. Is social media changing children’s brains? Here’s what the science says

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Bianca Nogrady is a freelance science journalist based in the Blue Mountains, west of Sydney, Australia.

Scientists say it is important to foster digital literacy and healthy online habits in those growing up using social media.Credit: StockPlanets/E+/Getty

In 1972, sociologist and criminologist Stanley Cohen published a book called Folk Devils and Moral Panics, which explored the concept of moral panic: the idea that societies periodically fixate on a newly emerged condition, behaviour, identity or community as being a threat to the public. The fixation is characterized by ‘handwringing’ and calls to action among societal leaders; a particular pattern of media coverage; and experts breaking down the problem and offering diagnoses and solutions.

Today, concerns about the impact of digital and social media on children and adolescents are never far from the headlines, but there is growing evidence that this isn’t simply another case of moral panic. Politicians, religious leaders and others have been speaking out with increasing intensity about how social media harms young people. And a growing volume of scientific literature is exploring the nature and prevalence of those harms, and what might be done about them1,2.

One thing that differentiates this case from moral panic is that young people themselves are worried, too. “It is not just older generations saying, ‘Kids, get off your screens’,” says Georgia Turner, a neuroscience researcher at the MRC Cognition and Brain Sciences Unit at the University of Cambridge, UK. Work by Turner and her colleagues suggests that nearly half of adolescents think that they are addicted to social media.

“Whether or not they are correct about the use of the clinical terms, they are clearly unhappy with their screen use,” Turner says. “I would say that we should treat people believing that they have a problem as itself a problem or a concern that we need to try and understand.”

Scientists have directed considerable effort into understanding the nature of screen addiction. “We know that the adolescent period is a time of profound changes in how the brain is developing and responding to its social environment, to peers, to family context,” says psychologist and neuroscientist Eva Telzer, co-director of the Winston National Center on Technology Use, Brain, and Psychological Development at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. And now, during that important developmental stage, adolescents are spending more time on digital technology, and in particular on social media.

Concerned about how social media might be affecting children and adolescents, governments around the world are attempting to regulate or curtail its use. Last December, the Australian government implemented a social-media ban for those aged under 16, intended to prevent them from accessing or having accounts on social-media platforms including Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and X. Numerous European countries, including the United Kingdom, France and Italy, are attempting to follow suit.

The situation raises a fundamental question, Telzer says: “How can this social environment potentially be rewiring the developing brain during this really important period when the brain is so sensitive?”

From birth, the brain grows rapidly in size and connectivity as children learn and develop and neurons proliferate and form connections called synapses. But in early childhood, that growth is accompanied by what’s called synaptic pruning, during which neuronal synapses disconnect and are cleared away. At the end of this process, there are around 40% fewer synapses than at the beginning. Neurons also die in a process called apoptosis. At the same time, the remaining neurons in the brain build up their coat of insulating white matter, or myelin, which is crucial for efficient transmission of electrical impulses.

While synaptic pruning is happening, the adolescent brain is maturing one region at a time, and the order of that maturation doesn’t lend itself to calm and rational thought and behaviour.

The first region to mature is rich in receptors for the hormone oxytocin — which is important in social bonding — and dopamine, a neurotransmitter associated with reward and pleasure. “It’s why every middle-school student wants to talk about who sits where in the cafeteria and who’s more popular than whom,” says Mitch Prinstein, a psychologist at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.

The last brain region to develop is the prefrontal cortex, which is essential for decision-making, exercising judgement and processing emotions such as fear and happiness.

Unfortunately, that makes the adolescent brain vulnerable to some design elements of social media: comparison features such as likes, and addictive elements such as push notifications and endless scrolling. “Imagine in the 80s, there was skywriting across your neighbourhood that said the most popular kid in school is talking about you right now with most of the rest of the grade in your school,” Prinstein says. “You would run down the street looking for them in your neighbourhood — it would be impossible to resist that.”

Neuroscience researcher Georgia Turner says that adolescents can be sensitive to the dopamine-driven rewards offered by social media.

And that is exactly what social media does for adolescents, he says, describing it as a perfect, tragic storm. “This is what the brain is hypersensitive towards, while not able to stop itself because the prefrontal cortex — the brain’s brakes — are not fully developed until the mid-20s,” Prinstein says.

A big part of the problem is dopamine, a neurotransmitter implicated in a range of addiction disorders. Because of the order in which brain regions mature, adolescents are extremely sensitive and responsive to reward, and social media delivers that in abundance; every like, new follower, positive comment or interesting thing delivers a kick of dopamine, says Turner. We experience those rewards in real life, but at a much lower frequency than on social media.

And that poses a risk to the developing brain. “We do know that if you, for example, do really increase dopamine transmission, that can have massive effects — particularly at young ages – on the way that your brain matures, and then your cognitive control in adulthood, your inhibition, your sensitivity to rewards,” Turner says.

Telzer and a colleague carried out a study involving 79 children and adolescents and found that those who spent more time on their smartphones during school hours — most of it on social media — performed worse on a test that assessed how well they could control their focus and attention. The researchers suggested that the immediate rewards offered by social media could be conditioning adolescents to need constant stimulation, and as a result they find it harder to maintain focus3.

Another study, co-authored by Samson Nivins, a developmental neuroscientist at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, which followed more than 8,300 children for four years, found a linear relationship between social-media use and inattention symptoms4.

Researchers have also used imaging to look for brain changes associated with social-media use. Nivins and his colleagues used magnetic resonance imaging to look for brain changes linked to using social media, playing video games or watching television over four years in 1,462 participants in the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study5. They found that children with higher social-media use showed a small but significant decrease in the volume of the cerebellum, a brain region that is known for coordinating movement and balance and that has a key role in cognition, memory and communication. “Why we are concerned is … the cerebellum is involved in all psychiatric disorders,” Nivins says, suggesting that this could be one mechanism underpinning the association between high social-media use and anxiety and depression.

Developmental neuroscientist Samson Nivins has used imaging techniques to explore how different types of screen use affect the developing brain.Credit: Senthil Kumar/Aswath Photo Studio

Social-media-linked disruptions to sleep in adolescents could also affect the formation of insulating myelin, a component of the brain’s white matter, which is crucial for efficient nerve conduction and healthy brain function. Poor sleep is associated with negative effects on the formation and maintenance of myelin. Research involving 976 children in the Adolescent Behavior Cognitive Development Study found an association between shorter sleep, worse white-matter organization, screen time and depressive symptoms in early adolescents. The paper also suggested that sleep duration and its effects on white matter mediated the association between increased social-media use and greater depression-related symptoms6. “Social media is the number-one reason why kids are not getting recommended sleep,” Prinstein says.

#816. Martha Stewart Blames Craig Melvin for Her Homeless Halloween Costume

Martha Stewart touched on the topic of her controversial Halloween costume, explaining that her appearance alongside Craig Melvin on Today accidentally caused the costume.

Martha Stewart didn’t mean to cause a stir.

Days after the lifestyle guru received backlash for posting a photo of herself dressed as a homeless person for Halloween, she explained her thought process behind the costume, claiming it was the result of Today host Craig Melvin accidentally getting chocolate on her during the show’s Oct. 30 episode.

“He spilled chocolate all over my white sweater, which I was gonna wear on Halloween night,” Stewart said at the CrossCountry Mortgage Sales Rally in Orlando Nov. 3, per footage obtained by TMZ. “When I picked up the sweater, I said, ‘Oh god, it’s so dirty. I only have 10 minutes to get dressed for this Halloween party.’”

“So the easiest costume was to get dressed up as a bum,” the 85-year-old continued. “I looked at myself and I said, ‘You really look hungry and homeless,’ so I wrote a sign that said, ‘I’m hungry.’ And boy, did that go off.”

E! News has reached out to Melvin’s reps for comment but has not heard back.

On the Halloween episode of Today, Stewart led a cooking demonstration in a recreation of her 2026 Winter Olympics look, while Melvin dressed as her longtime friend Snoop Dogg. As Melvin reached for the chocolate ganache, he accidentally spilled some on Stewart.

“Real Snoop would never do that,” she playfully chided, to which Melvin quickly replied, “So sorry, Martha.”

Amid criticism over Stewart’s Halloween costume—which included a beanie, ragged jeans and a plaid button-up under a torn cardigan with dirt smeared across her face—the cookbook author deleted the photo from Instagram and expressed remorse for causing controversy.

“I’ve spent decades teaching others how to celebrate Halloween,”  she said in a statement to People on Nov. 1, “sharing fun, festive recipes, providing unique craft ideas and giving tips on entertaining and hosting to make the most of one of my favorite holidays of the year.”

“I am distressed that my Halloween costume yesterday, which was intended to bring more awareness to the very serious subject of homelessness, has offended people,” she continued, “which was never my intention.”

The TV personality also issued another apology on Instagram, which has since been deleted.

“It’s hard to admit when you’ve really screwed up,” she wrote, per Entertainment Weekly. “My earlier statement didn’t go far enough. I know many people are suffering economically. Wearing a costume like I did was insensitive and not funny. I am very sorry.”

For a look at more of Stewart’s shocking confessions over the years, keep reading.

Martha Stewart—then still Martha Kostyra—lost her virginity when she was 19, to her future husband Andrew Stewart, a student at Yale Law School.

“He was very aggressive,” the lifestyle mogul said in the 2024 Netflix documentary Martha, “and I liked it.”

Martha Stewart Kissed Another Man—on Her Honeymoon

It wasn’t a harbinger of good things to come, but Martha maintained that kissing another man while she and Andrew were honeymooning in Europe after their 1961 nuptials wasn’t that big a deal.

“It was neither naughty nor unfaithful,” she said in Martha of smooching the stranger at a cathedral on Easter eve in Florence, Italy. “It was just emotional, of the moment. That’s how I looked at it. And it was exciting. I wish we could all experience such an evening.”

Martha Stewart Cheated on Husband Andrew Stewart

Martha admitted in the documentary to a “very brief affair” with “a very attractive Irish man” during her time working as a stockbroker in the late 1960s.

“I would have never broken up a marriage for it,” she said. “It was nothing. It was like the kiss in the cathedral.”

She insinuated that Andrew was repeatedly unfaithful, despite her ex-husband maintaining he didn’t cheat until she confessed her infidelity.

“I didn’t go run off with people. He was running off with people,” she said. “I always said I was a swan and like all swans, they are monogamous.”

Being a Mom Wasn’t a Natural Fit for Martha Stewart

Martha had to work at honing her maternal instincts when her daughter Alexis Stewart was born in 1965.

“Back then, everybody was having babies so young,” she reflected in Martha. “That was sort of the style and the habit. I thought it was a natural thing, and it turns out it’s not at all nature to be a mother.”

While she and Alexis remain close, Martha told People in 2020, “I tried to involve her in everything, but the minute she could leave home and go to boarding school, she did. Our relationship has always been a difficult mother-daughter relationship. Difficult, but she would do anything for me, and I would do anything for her."

Martha infamously served five months at FPC Alderson after being convicted in 2004 of conspiracy, obstruction and lying to federal investigators in connection with an insider trading case.

At one point she was punished for touching a female guard’s “big silver key chain” after complimenting how nice the guard looked, as she shared in Martha, having momentarily forgotten the prison rules.

She ended up “dragged into solitary for ‘touching an officer,’” Martha said. “No food or water for a day. This was ‘Camp Cupcake,’ remember?”

Martha Stewart’s Thoughts on Hosting a Talk Show

Upon her release in March 2005, as Martha put it in the doc, she “had to climb out of a f--king hole”—and daytime TV seemed like a step in that direction.

But while she’s been the face of countless endeavors over the years, onscreen and off, hosting Martha for seven seasons, she said, “was more like prison than being at Alderson.”

Martha said on a February 2024 episode of her eponymous podcast that she never had a facelift, but her dermatologist Dr. Daniel Belkin did inject Botox in her neck and along her jawline and put filler in her cheeks and jawline.

Belkin noted that they had also done ultrasound-based skin tightening, and she recalled having a Fraxel laser treatment on her body.

"My décolletage and across my chest looks so good now," Martha told the doctor. "That is a combination of your work and Pilates." She further chalked up her radiant visage to clean eating—her daily green juice ingredients come straight from her garden, naturally—and staying active.

Martha Stewart Enjoys Snoop Dogg’s Contact High

While she didn’t partake herself, Martha felt “fabulous” when her friend and frequent cohost Snoop Dogg smoked weed around her, she shared when he was a guest on the 2022 premiere of her podcast.

“It makes me feel really good," she confessed. "It does not disturb my concentration. In fact, I think it makes it even better and it doesn't make me tired or any of the things people say marijuana does to you. It's fantastic, I think it's great."

The Alcohol Martha Stewart Hadn’t Tasted Since College

Martha loves a craft cocktail, but there’s one spirit that has haunted her since she was a student at Barnard.

“I got so drunk on gin in college,” she told Snoop in 2024 at Food Network's New York City Wine & Food Festival, “that I have not ever had gin since.”

"But," she told her friend, who inevitably entered the alcohol market with the drink he's been linked to for 30 years, "I can’t wait to taste your Gin & Juice!”

Incidentally, though Martha is practically synonymous with white wine, she is not a day drinker.

“I never drink it before dinner, ever," she told The Cut in 2017. "I couldn't function for a second if I had to drink it at lunchtime or something like that."

Why Martha Stewart Doesn’t Wear Underwear

Martha skips wearing underwear in lieu of having her swimsuit on at all times—just in case she feels like taking a dip.

"Bathing suits are my underwear," the 2023 Sports Illustrated Swimsuit Issue cover girl told Page Six in 2024. "I don't wear any of that structured stuff. No tight lace. I don't wear those. I only wear Eres bathing suits under my clothes."

Martha Stewart’s One-Night Stand Confession

On Watch What Happens Live! in 2013, the answer was “yes” when Andy Cohen asked if Martha ever had a one-night stand. She had also sexted, FYI, and her answer to whether she’d ever had a threesome was a smirking “maybe.”
