#727. ‘Fruitcakes: Dawn of Drag’ Goes Back to ‘Happy Gays,’ “Reclaiming History” Through a Timely Film (Exclusive Trailer and Chat)

Finnish filmmaker Vesa Kuosmanen discusses his doc, premiering at Tallinn, how it feels like a story for our time amid a backlash against trans and queer rights, and how fear drives anger.

Happy Gays. That was the name of Finland’s first drag show in the late 1970s, which drew big, loud and proud audiences. Among the people on stage back then were Mummo, one of the first openly gay men in the country, and his best friend Jolanda. Now, you can relive, or experience for the first time, some of the excitement of those days in the new documentary Fruitcakes: Dawn of Drag, which will celebrate its world premiere during the 30th edition of the Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF) in Estonia.

But it isn’t all about fun and panache. After all, not everyone was happy to hear about the now-legendary drag show and its performers’ joy back in the day. And when the AIDS crisis hit, fear and violence were among the responses. In 1988, Mummo was killed in his home in Helsinki. Related Stories TV Sophie Stone Has Been Writing a Play and a Sitcom and Says, "There's So Much to Gain" From Our Differences Movies 'Sounds of the Desert' Explores Lives, Music and Cosmic Visions of Two Members of the Sun Ra Arkestra (Exclusive Tallinn Trailer)

Finnish filmmaker Vesa Kuosmanen (Just Animals) has a view of that building from a window in his apartment. Amid the more recent backlash against queer rights, he started thinking about making a film about that not-so-distant past.

He met the aforementioned Jolanda, a retired archivist. More than 30 years after his friend’s death, Jolanda opened up his own archive for Fruitcakes: Dawn of Drag. And the filmmaker and Jolanda invited a new generation of drag artists to bring Happy Gays back to the stage. The heartwarming film takes us on a ride through archive and new footage and rehearsals and re-enactments of Happy Gays that bring up happy but also painful memories, along with a different side of the at times curmudgeonly Jolanda. And it puts a spotlight on drag’s power to bring people together, to celebrate and to endure discrimination.

Kuosmanen also wrote the film and edited it together with Jussi Sandhu, with cinematography courtesy of Mikko Kelloniemi. Rise and Shine has boarded the film and is handling world sales. “Fruitcakes is much more than only a very entertaining trip down memory lane of drag culture in the 1980s,” says Rise and Shine’s Anja Dziersk. “It is a masterpiece of Finnish humor, connected to a very timely message as we see queer life being challenged and threatened every day.”

THR can premiere a colorful and music-driven trailer for the film right here. Put your dancing shoes on!

Ahead of the Saturday world premiere of Fruitcakes: Dawn of Drag in Tallinn’s Doc@PÖFF International Competition program, THR talked to Kuosmanen about how the film came about, the early days of Finnish drag, mixing sorrow and joy, and why the doc’s title is about “reclaiming history” and language.

The filmmaker says a key inspiration for the film came a few years ago when the ice hockey-obsessed Finland won the world championship in the sport. “We rarely have such collective joy,” he says. “I’m not a big fan of ice hockey at all, but I think it’s lovely that people come out into the streets and celebrate. But then I heard that my friends were beaten up by ice hockey fans just because they look different.” And there were news stories about violence against people in the trans community.

Kuosmanen started thinking about what causes such anger. “My conclusion was it’s fear,” he tells THR. “It’s a fear of difference. So, I had this political motive for [exploring] how fear creates anger. And in our time of social media, we talk about how the algorithm pushes anger forward, and I think that’s completely true. But the real problem is actually fear. That there’s so much fear created, and we respond to fear through anger. So, I wanted to find out more about the story of Mummo’s murder.”

Finding people who remembered that time and were willing to discuss it proved difficult. “It almost felt like it was a forgotten history of Finland,” the filmmaker shares.

Then he was introduced to Jolanda, 70, who “kept all the archives and every single newspaper clip – basically everything,” the director tells THR. “So I went to meet him, but he was the most unlikely documentary protagonist ever because he really didn’t want to be in the film and was really crumpy, with a cynical sense of humor. He also refuses to use the pronouns she/her. But I kept going to his place to scan documents and chat, and we became friends fairly quickly.”

Jolanda’s personality also fit the director’s interest in authenticity. “I personally dislike the righteous heroes who are staring from the window and are doing the right thing all the time,” Kuosmanen tells THR. “He’s this pioneer who has done great things but is a flawed human being. I didn’t want to make a film from my point of view [a la], ‘Look at these heroes.’ I wanted to show them as the more complex human [beings that they are].”

Complex was also the process of putting together visuals for the film. After all, Jolanda is so proud of the Happy Gay show, but beyond some footage that the filmmaker found in the archives of the Finnish public broadcaster, there wasn’t enough video material, which led the creative team to the idea of a reenactment of the legendary show.

“That gave me the form of the film, which happened fairly organically,” Kuosmanen recalls. “I started with this political motive, then I found this amazing character, and then we started pairing the young, woke drag artists with the older generation.”

What he found, and what audiences will see in Fruitcakes, is that the drag pioneers and the younger generation differ in their focus and way of expressing themselves. “The older people have a more honest attitude to life, in a way, while it feels that the younger generation is so polished and has thought everything through,” Kuosmanen tells THR. “So we started creating more situations where we could film them together, because the meeting point of generations became a key part of the film. These interactions really talked to me and touched my heart. So, it went from a very political [approach], became a more personal and character-driven piece, and then we added this more conceptual, cross- generational thing.”

Fruitcakes shows Jolanda missing Mummo but doesn’t go into much depth on the latter’s murder. “That was really important for me because I think that when you portray queer violence, in a way it creates more violence,” the Finnish filmmaker tells THR. “There have been so many films where queer people get killed. So I really wanted to be careful that it would not be one of those.”

The emotional core of the film combines “the long-lasting impact of sorrow and pain that Lolanda feels” and smiles, dancing and joy, Kuosmanen highlights. “For me, it’s all about celebration amidst the most horrible things happening,” he tells THR. “I think it’s super important that we don’t close our eyes to the world, but we need to embrace the whole cosmos of life, and that includes having parties, having a good time, going out to bars, kissing people. We must be able to have agency. And we shouldn’t forget joy.”

So, how did the filmmaker choose the title of his doc? “It’s difficult to find names that don’t sound too pretentious, so I think it’s good to have a little bit of a wink” in the title, Kuosmanen shares. “I feel that the title is much more like the original Happy Gays. For me, it’s about reclaiming history, reclaiming something. ‘Queer’ used to be a word you weren’t supposed to use, and now we are calling ourselves ‘queer.’ So, it’s really about reclaiming history in the sense that it’s us who define what we can be called and what language we use. And I love the playfulness of it.”

#726. Carrie Coon Dubs Taylor Swift ‘So Bertha,’ While Praising Singer’s Spot-On Impression of her ‘Gilded Age’ Character

The actress said family matriarch Bertha Russell is a 19th century version of Swift.

Taylor Swift has made moves both behind and in front of the camera, but according to actress Carrie Coon, the singer might have yet another sideline as a professional impressionist. During an appearance on The Tonight Show on Wednesday (Nov. 4), Coon had the highest of praise for Swift’s impression of her character Bertha Russell from The Gilded Age. Explore Taylor Swift See latest videos, charts and news

“It’s very good,” Coon said clapping as host Jimmy Fallon played back the clip from Swift’s Oct. 2025 spot on his show in which she playfully made fun of the way she and pal Selena Gomez used to dress as teenagers by slipping into her Bertha impression. Coon said she did not see the bit when it aired, but woke up the next morning to “thousands” of text and Instagram messages about it. Related Cher Hits Michael Douglas With Kindness After Actor's 'Moonstruck' Oscar Diss Hailey Bieber Details Emotional Rollercoaster of PMDD Diagnosis After Son Jack Blues' Birth: 'Just a Really Intense and Special Journey' Barbie's Diwali Doll Is Back in Stock for the Festival of Lights: Here's Where to Find It Online

“People were like, ‘Can you believe it?,’ you know. And I have to say it’s very good,” Coon said of Swift’s take on her character. “It’s the right affectation. And she’s so Bertha, she’s such an entrepreneur. Bertha would be like Taylor Swift if she was living today.”

During her appearance last year, Swift was talking about how happy she was for pal Gomez’s marriage to producer Benny Blanco and recalled that she did some “light teasing” at the couple’s wedding about the clothes she and Gomez wore back in the day, delivered, naturally, in the voice of her favorite Gilded Age character.

“It was quite a year, let me tell you,” Swift said in Bertha’s practiced, theatrical mid-Atlantic accent on The Tonight Show. “It was the year of deep, deep v-necks.” The singer said she dropped into her Gilded Age voice because she just loves the show so much. “It was the year of aggressively colorful skinny jeans,” she continued in the accent. “Everyone was walking around saying things were amazeballs. Mrs. Astor hated it.”

When Fallon asked Coon if she thought Swift would ever appear on The Gilded Age, the actress said she thinks she “should,” noting that Swift was “really great” in a Law & Order: SVU bit she appeared in at this year’s Emmy Awards. “I feel like she’d be an excellent nemesis [for Bertha]. Best friend? Maybe best friend. She can help me defeat Enid Winterton.”

To date, Swift has had several screen roles, including a cameo on New Girl, as well as bit parts in 2010’s Valentine’s Day, a voice part in 2012’s The Lorax, a starring role in 2014’s The Giver, a turn at playing flirtatious feline Bombalurina in the bomb big-screen live action version of Cats and an appearance in the 2022 David O. Russell film Amsterdam, among others.

#725. Carbon radical generation by irreversible metal-to-ligand charge transfer

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

We’re sharing this article early to provide faster access to peer-reviewed, accepted research. It is citable and carries a permanent DOI. This version is subject to further edits and will be replaced automatically by the final Version of Record. All legal disclaimers apply.

Metal-to-ligand charge transfer (MLCT) is a fundamental photoinduced process that underpins a broad range of energy- or electron-transfer events1,2. In the absence of productive substrate engagement, the MLCT excited state typically relaxes to the ground state via photophysical deactivation, reflecting its largely reversible character3,4. Here we report a class of isolable copper–heteroaryl sulfone complexes that, upon visible light irradiation, undergo an irreversible MLCT-driven fragmentation through C–S bond cleavage within the coordinated sulfone ligand, generating carbon-centered radicals. Spectroscopic and computational studies support the formation of MLCT-derived excited states and a low-barrier pathway for C–S bond cleavage. This reactivity is largely independent of the reduction potentials of the corresponding free sulfones, enabling the generation of fluoroalkyl and non-fluorinated tertiary, secondary, and primary (even methyl) alkyl radicals. We demonstrate the utility of this platform in copper-catalyzed C–H fluoroalkylation of arenes and terminal alkynes. Leveraging these MLCT-generated trifluoromethyl radicals to initiate halogen-atom transfer (XAT) from perfluorocyclobutyl iodide (I-FCB), we also achieve radical perfluorocyclobutylation–iodination of alkenes, addressing a longstanding challenge in the incorporation of perfluorocyclobutyl motifs.

#724. ‘Married at First Sight UK’ Canceled Amid Rape Claims, Review Finds “Implicit Pressure” on Contestants to Be Intimate

CEO Priya Dogra has decided that the "right course was to bring 'MAFS UK' on Channel 4 to an end."

Channel 4 has canceled Married at First Sight UK after two contestants claimed they had been raped during the filming of the show.

That decision was unveiled despite an external review giving the green light to produce future installments with improvements to the welfare framework. The suggestions for Channel 4 and production company CPL included installing CCTV, putting locks in shared bedrooms, and giving contestants access to a panic button.

“Whilst the review praised the welfare protocols in place and made no findings that Channel 4 breached the Ofcom Code or that the format is inherently unsafe, I have to consider when is the right time for Channel 4 to move on from a format,” said the broadcaster’s CEO Priya Dogra. “The recommendations are eminently sensible and feasible, but considering their wholesale implementation provoked fundamental questions about the editorial proposition of a show that, I believe, has now run its course over ten years.” Related Stories Movies 'Fruitcakes: Dawn of Drag' Goes Back to 'Happy Gays,' "Reclaiming History" Through a Timely Film (Exclusive Trailer and Chat) TV Sophie Stone Has Been Writing a Play and a Sitcom and Says, "There's So Much to Gain" From Our Differences

Earlier this year, a group of ex-participants came forward in a BBC Panorama investigation, where it came to light that two women on MAFS UK — where singletons are matched, by experts, with a stranger and meet for the first time at a mock wedding — alleged violent attacks.

The first said her husband had raped her and later threatened her with an acid attack, while a second woman told Channel 4 and CPL before broadcast about being allegedly raped by her husband. Her episodes, according to the BBC program, were still aired. A third woman, Shona Manderson, the only one to have revealed her identity, accused her onscreen husband of a non-consensual sex act. The men involved deny the claims, challenging the details of each woman’s account.

All of the former participants who spoke to the BBC said Channel 4 did not do enough to protect them. The BBC reported at the time that Channel 4 was aware of some allegations before broadcast, but had previously told Panorama that all of the claims were “wholly uncorroborated and disputed.” The broadcaster did, however, pull all episodes of the program from its streaming and linear services.

On Thursday, Channel 4 released the findings of an external review into the show, split into two parts: A review by law firm Clyde & Co, and a future-facing review by former Controller of BBC One, Lorraine Heggessey. Channel 4 stated at the top of the document that it is “not in a position to investigate or adjudicate on the […] allegations as those would be for the police and the courts to investigate and determine.”

But the reviews could examine the welfare protocols in place on the relevant series of MAFS UK, the welfare concerns referenced in the Panorama program, and the handling of Channel 4 and production company CPL of those concerns when raised — and whether all of that fulfilled Channel 4’s duty of care obligations under Britain’s Ofcom Broadcasting Code.

The Clyde & Co findings essentially found that the welfare framework on MAFS UK was in place at the relevant times and was compliant with Ofcom’s Broadcasting Code. There were no findings of a breach of the code, but Clyde & Co did uncover areas where it considered that the contributor welfare framework “although compliant, could be further strengthened.” For example, they found that some contestants were discovered with prohibited substances but were “given a first and final warning rather than being removed from the programme.”

Heggessey’s findings were much more substantial. It concluded that, with “enhancements” to the existing welfare framework, it would “be reasonable to produce future series of MAFS UK.” And while it observed that Channel 4 and CPL take contributor welfare “extremely seriously,” there is room for improvement.

Heggessey called into question a number of the procedures, including that the premise of the show — to match contributors with long-term partners — heightens tension and conflict, with intimacy being a key focus. “Although some of this is necessary from a welfare perspective, for example during welfare checks, some elements of the show could implicitly put pressure on contributors to be intimate,” the review said. Because contact with the outside world is limited during filming, contributors can become dependent on production and “lose touch with reality,” which can affect their decision-making, the report claimed.

Contestant background checks and contributors’ “motivations” for participating on the show were also raised in the findings. “While the close involvement and influence of Channel 4 has some benefit, it has at times led to a lack of objective scrutiny over some production decisions,” said the Heggessey review.

Her recommendations included putting the couples in separate bedrooms on the wedding night and honeymoon and turning the honeymoon into a “getting to know you” phase, with the couples subsequently having to “opt in” to share a room. She also said Channel 4 and CPL should review the frequency with which couples are asked about the physical side of their relationship and remove Intimacy Week and Partner Swap Week.

MAFS is Love Island-esque in its global popularity, with localized versions in over 35 countries. The U.K. series has been running for 10 seasons now and often boasts viewership of over three million, making it one of Britain’s most prized reality shows.

No one knew what it looked like until the day before Halloween, when the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico captured the first radar images.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On October 31, 2015, an asteroid shaped like a human skull flew by Earth. It arrived with excellent timing on Halloween, which made the already-creepy asteroid even creepier.

During its closest approach, the creepy asteroid was about 300,000 miles from Earth, or 1.3 times the average distance between Earth and the moon. So, it didn't pose a threat to our planet. It was discovered by astronomers at Hawaii's Pan-STARRS observatory only three weeks before the flyby, and it was given the official designation "2015 TB145." But no one knew what it looked like until the day before Halloween, when the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico captured the first radar images.

NASA called the asteroid the "Great Pumpkin," while others called it the "Halloween Asteroid."

Be afraid, be very afraid... Okay, not really, but there is reason to be concerned about near-Earth objects and the time in which they are detected.

"According to the catalog of near-Earth objects (NEOs) kept by the Minor Planet Center, this is the closest currently known approach by an object this large until asteroid 1999 AN10, at about 2,600 feet (800 meters) in size, approaches at about 1 lunar distance (238,000 miles from Earth) in August 2027," NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) reported in 2015.

NASA’s Near-Earth Object Observations Program, sometimes called “Spaceguard,” works to catalog these type of objects and predicts some of their paths if they could be potentially threats to our planet. While there are no known credible impact threats to date, it doesn't mean the "Great Pumpkin," or rather a great impactor, isn't real.

As for 2015 TB145, it did return to Earth's vicinity in 2018, but at a much more distant pass of about 24 million miles (38 million kilometers), "or about a quarter the distance between Earth and the sun," according to JPL.

Hanneke joined the Space.com team in 2016 as a staff writer and producer, covering topics including spaceflight and astronomy. She currently lives in Seattle, home of the Space Needle, with her cat and two snakes. #722. 2026 CMA Awards Announce Kacey Musgraves, Ella Langley, Tim McGraw & More Performers, Plus Dolly Parton Tribute

Nov. 18 show will also include performances from Cody Johnson, Miranda Lambert, The Red Clay Strays, Zach Top & Tucker Wetmore.

The upcoming 60th annual CMA Awards performer lineup is set to include a string of hitmakers, fan favorites, and a newly minted Country Music Hall of Famer.

The first round of CMA Awards performers includes Kacey Musgraves, Cody Johnson, Miranda Lambert, The Red Clay Strays, Zach Top and Tucker Wetmore, as well as Ella Langley, whose “Choosin’ Texas” has dominated the all-genre Billboard Hot 100 this year. The initial performer lineup reveal also features Tim McGraw, who was just inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame last month.

The CMAs will also pay tribute to late Country Music Hall of Fame member Dolly Parton, who died in August.

Reigning CMA entertainer of the year Lainey Wilson will host the CMA Awards for a third consecutive year. The awards show will air live from Nashville’s Bridgestone Arena on Wednesday, Nov. 18, on ABC and Disney+ and will be available the following day on Hulu.

Langley leads this year’s nominees with nine nods, including entertainer, album (Dandelion), female vocalist, musical event and music video of the year, as well as two nominations for single and song of the year.

Johnson, the reigning CMA male vocalist of the year, is up for four CMA Awards trophies, including entertainer, male vocalist, single and music video of the year. Lambert has seven nominations this year, among them two for single of the year and her 19th nomination for female vocalist of the year (with 70 career nominations, Lambert also holds the record for the most CMA Awards nominations by a female artist). Musgraves has five nominations heading into the awards ceremony, among them album (Middle of Nowhere), female vocalist and song of the year.

The Red Clay Strays are the reigning vocal group of the year and look to retain their title this year. Zach Top, the reigning new artist of the year, is nominated twice heading into this year’s awards ceremony, including male vocalist of the year and album of the year (Ain’t In It for My Health). Wetmore picks up his second CMA Awards nomination this year in the new artist of the year category.

Last year’s CMA Awards winners also included Wilson taking home album of the year for Whirlwind, Langley and Riley Green’s “You Look Like You Love Me” earning song and single of the year, and the Post Malone and Blake Shelton collaboration “Pour Me a Drink” being named musical event of the year.

#721. Volkswagen logs Q3 operating loss of €5.86 billion on Porsche writedown

The Volkswagen Group has filed its worst quarterly performance since the height of the "Dieselgate" scandal in 2015. Share prices climbed in response, however, perhaps because the bad news was so well signposted.

The Volkswagen Group on Thursday posted its worst quarterly numbers in more than a decade.

The company reported an operating loss of €5.86 billion (roughly $6.53 billion) during July, August and September. One-off costs, not least a massive writedown in its stake in struggling sister company Porsche, explained the vast bulk of the losses.

The world's second-largest carmaker is battling mounting competition from and falling demand in the core Chinese market.

It is pursuing a major restructuring and downsizing program, trying to bolster falling profit margins, and executives said the difficulties highlighted the urgency of this process.

"The nine-month results make one thing clear: We cannot afford to lose any time. We must act quickly and decisively," chief financial officer Arno Antlitz said in a video statement.

The results were the latest reminder of the pressure on VW — and the wider German and Western automotive industry — to react to increasing competition in China, high costs and practical difficulties moving towards electric car production, and unpredictable and rising tariff burdens, thanks in no small part to US President Donald Trump.

And here are some of the key year-to-date 9-month figures:

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

VW shares were already at their lowest levels in well over 10 years prior to Thursday's announcements, after months of difficult headlines and the ongoing plans to shed tens of thousands of jobs and reduce production capacities.

Perhaps as a result of this, the stock dipped briefly as markets opened and the news was published, but then started to rally as the day progressed.

By midday in Frankfurt, VW shares had climbed by 2% compared to their prices at the start of trading on the DAX.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

CEO Oliver Blume plans to shed around 100,000 jobs across the group, which includes the Audi and Porsche brands, in the coming years though a combination of layoffs and not replacing departing or retiring personnel.

Multiple factors are contributing to this. They include increased competition from Chinese manufacturers, falling revenues in China, changeable US auto tariffs under President Donald Trump, different staffing requirements when manufacturing electric cars and difficulties moving towards making and selling more electric cars at the pace once designated by political leaders.

Up to four plants in Germany could face closure as part of the plan, which has met with considerable union resistance and could lead to strikes starting next year.

CFO Antlitz said the figures showed the urgency underlying these plans, saying the company needed to increase its profit margins by 2030 to solidify its finances.

Antlitz said the operating return on sales was only 3.8% in the first nine months of the year, even before the one-off writedowns hitting the bottom line.

"That is not enough in the long term," he said.

As part of its restructuring program, the VW Group aims to restore an operating profit margin of between 8-10% by 2030.

This year, amid one-off costs now totaling in the region of €10 billion, it expects a profit margin of no more than 1%, compared to prior forecasts in the region of 5%.

On Episode 234 of This Week In Space, Tariq Malik and Mike Wall are joined by Than Putzig of the Planetary Science Institute about a NASA-backed payload bound for the Marius Hills Pit on the moon.

In our ongoing quest to develop a moon base, could we possibly utilize the area beneath the surface of the moon in order to make the moon habitable? Could Marius Hills Pit, a roughly 50-meter-wide opening that may lead into a lunar lava tube, become the Moon's first living habitat for humans?

Putzig explains how geophysical instruments on a rover could detect hidden voids beneath the surface and measure the size of these lava tubes. We also ask Than how these lava tubes form, what a follow-up robotic explorer could reveal, and how this research fits alongside NASA’s Artemis plans for a south polar moon base. Join us!

#718. Cristian Castro Signs With Enso Music for Management: ‘Chance to Build Something Truly Historic’

The news comes shortly after the Mexican icon was honored with a Billboard Lifetime Achievement Award.

Cristian Castro, who was recently honored with a Billboard Lifetime Achievement Award, has signed a management deal with Enso Music, Billboard can exclusively announce on Thursday (Nov. 5). The new partnership opens a new chapter in the celebrated career of the Mexican pop icon, now under the guidance of renowned Latin music executive Jorge Juárez.

“Cristian is one of the most important and recognizable artists in Latin music, with a voice and a catalog that have transcended generations and borders,” Juárez, CEO of Enso Music, said in a statement. “It’s a privilege to begin this new chapter together and to welcome, here at Enso Music, an artist with such a rich history who is also experiencing an extraordinary moment in his career. We share a vision of continuing to build, to grow, and to take his music to new stages and audiences around the world.”

Meanwhile, Castro celebrated his arrival at the company and expressed being “deeply grateful” for the trust that Juárez and his team have placed in him for the next chapter of his career, which includes a new album slated for 2027 and the continuation of his Nada Solo Éxitos Tour, which began on Sept. 11 in Las Vegas and will run through March 2027.

“Some opportunities go far beyond a signature. They represent hope, excitement, dreams and the chance to build something truly historic, an unrepeatable mark along the way,” he said. “Thank you for believing in me, opening doors for me and making me feel wanted and cared for. My commitment is to give my very best, work with passion and rise to the occasion. Thank you for making this joy possible today. On the horizon, I see great achievements and many successes we’ll share together.”

With more than 12 million albums sold, Castro, who has established himself as one of the defining voices of Latin pop and romantic music, began his Billboard chart journey in 1992 when “No Podrás” became his first entry on Hot Latin Songs, peaking at No. 3. His debut album, Agua Nueva, reached No. 2 on the Top Latin Pop Albums chart in January 1993, and since then, he has earned six No. 1s on Hot Latin Songs, including “Nunca Voy a Olvidarte,” “Amor” and “Azul,” which spent four, 11 and nine weeks at the top, respectively. In 2011, Viva El Príncipe, his tribute to legendary Mexican singer José José, spent seven weeks at No. 1 on Top Latin Albums.

On Oct. 22, Castro was celebrated at the Billboard Latin Music Awards with the Billboard Lifetime Achievement Award, recognizing an exceptional career spanning more than three decades and his enduring influence on Latin music. Today, he continues to connect with audiences through his Nada Solo Éxitos Tour, with performances at major venues such as the Auditorio Nacional in Mexico City and Madison Square Garden in New York.

#717. Imax Posts Record Revenue, Profit Growth With ‘The Odyssey’ in Third Quarter

Christopher Nolan's epic on its screens helped the film technologies company record best-ever key earnings metrics from a mix of Hollywood and local language titles.

Imax saw big gains from Christopher Nolan‘s The Odyssey on its screens as the film technologies company posted record global box office, revenue and profit growth in the third quarter.

Lifted by Hollywood’s ongoing recovery at the multiplex, Imax posted record quarterly global box office at $712 million during Q3, well up on a year-earlier $368 million. The big audience draw had been a 70mm run for Nolan’s epic as it contributed to premium ticket sales surpassing $550 million worldwide.

During the latest quarter, Imax saw revenue rise 64 percent to $174.6 million, compared to a year-earlier $106.7 million. Net income rose over 400 percent to $117.1 million, against $22.6 million in the same period of 2025. Related Stories Movies Cinemark Won't Screen Brad Pitt's 'Cliff Booth' Movie Over Netflix's Demands, CEO Says Movies Elon Musk's Anti-Woke AI 'The Odyssey' Movie Ripped as "Soulless Slop" After Criticizing Nolan

Adjusted EBITIDA hit $121 million, up 133 percent from a year-earlier $51.8 million, another quarterly record, as was the adjusted earnings per-share at $2.21, compared to a year-earlier 47 cents. “These results demonstrate the significant operating leverage and opportunity as we further expand the network and grow Imax box office,” Imax CFO Natasha Fernandes told analysts during a morning call. During the latest quarter, content solutions revenue rose 110 percent to $94 million in the third quarter, driven by the global box office increase, while technology products and services revenue increased 28 percent to $77 million.

Heading towards the end of 2026, Imax has the upcoming release of Dune: Part Three and the Chinese release of Avengers: Doomsday, and a 2027 slate to include movies shot with proprietary Imax cameras, including Star Wars: Starfighter, and the Superman sequel Man of Tomorrow. Avengers: Secret Wars and the Imax debut of the original Star Wars will be presented in 70mm film for the first time. Imax said it had already drawn $30 million in pre-sales for Dune: Part Three, its second highest pre-sales ever.

And after Imax merchandise for The Odyssey included a first-ever popular popcorn bucket, the company is rolling out a Godzilla Minus Zero apparel line, including a t-shirt, and has a line of Imax-branded products to target the December release of Dune: Part Three.

“What Imax achieved goes beyond simply a ‘great quarter’ and transcends the many records we shattered in the period. What we believe we are witnessing is an awakening to the power and potential of our platform to impact global culture, unlock new commercial opportunities, and inspire a new level of demand and awe in audiences around the world,” Rich Gelfond, CEO of Imax Corp., said in a statement on Thursday.

Imax forecasts it will exceed its 2026 full-year guidance for a record $1.4 billion in global box office after signing agreements for 105 theater systems worldwide so far this year. Gelfond on the morning analyst call pointed to a 13-theater agreement in Europe expected to shortly close and be announced.

Imax is also at work on pilots for new concept auditoriums, including smaller, ultra-premium venues for better immersive aspect ratio, depth of view and sound. Gelfond also said it is looking to expand its 70mm film locations by 10 to 15 new locations.

The Imax chief also touted the upcoming Imax release for the sequel to Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, the Brad Pitt-starrer The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth. Cinemark and Regal among major chains have decided against their own sequel releases due to Netflix’s ultra-short two-week release window on offer, while AMC Theatres will screen the David Fincher film, starring Brad Pitt, on its Imax screens.

Gelfond argued the Cliff Booth release on his screens “marks an exciting experiment for us, releasing across more than 550 Imax locations worldwide ahead of its debut on Netflix this Christmas.” Cliff Booth will debut in theaters on Nov. 25, then hit Netflix on Dec. 23.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Abandoned, possessed, or infested spaceships in sci-fi films, books, and video games are usually not a welcoming place to hang your helmet and kick back inside.

Many are distinctly marked as DO NOT APPROACH zones and equipped with clearly articulated warning messages to keep your distance, but that doesn't ever seem to stop scavengers, space pirates, or evil industrial mega corporations from waving off these dangerous signs to board anyway.

Other creaky craft are apt to contain nasty alien hitchhikers or biological hazards not exactly conducive to a pleasant star-trekking voyage. Whether these nefarious neglected craft have just reappeared from the other side of a black hole or have been lying dormant for eons on a hostile planetoid, visitors are usually infrequent.

So ignore those distress beacons at your own peril and step into this alarming armada of 9 nightmarish sci-fi spaceships before orbits decay.

This is not a ranked list, just a collection of our favorites.

It's basically a perfectly good interstellar mining vessel owned by the Concordance Extraction Corporation if you forget about the nasty reanimated corpses found lurking on nearly every deadly deck.

The pesky Necromorphs are a resilient crop of creatures and are extremely inhospitable when it comes to having uninvited guests, yet they don't mind if you're staying for dinner.

This plague of hungry zombified corpses is a real drag, unless you happen to have a flaring plasma cutter in your back pocket and your name is Isaac Clarke.

Things would be much more peaceful aboard the Grendel if a notorious undead slasher named Jason Voorhees wasn't stashed in the cargo bay, but when scientific discovery enters the equation, many questionable choices follow.

The Grendel is a 25th-century medical research vessel on a field trip from hell to an overly polluted Earth, where the frozen Jason is kept at the Crystal Lake Research Facility and shipped back home to Earth 2 for cellular research.

Once thawed, the ship becomes his private killing field with an ample supply of student bodies until the fiery finale when Jason becomes an inhuman meteor in the sky. Next time, take the school bus.

This spooky classic novel written by "2001's" legendary author, Arthur C. Clarke, focuses on a massive alien spaceship entering Earth's atmosphere.

The 31-mile-long cylindrical spaceship does not parallel park easily and is quite spacious inside. In fact, it’s primarily hollow at first and likely offers up a fantastic location for some echoey yodeling. As we later learn, Rama aliens are apparently collecting forms of intelligent life from around the galaxy, employing their ginormous Rama spacecraft.

As an ice ring thaws and forms a vast ocean, astronauts explore the ship’s cavernous confines, only to find automated bio-machines and weird metallic towers, curved alloy cliffs, and fantastic geometric city-like structures. The myriad mysteries that unfold are enough to drive sane humans to absolute madness!

Ignore that glistening brown protomolecular goo, and come on in and sit a spell in the Scopuli, a light Martian freighter used by the Outer Planets Alliance for clandestine missions and ransacked by the evil security firm Protogen in an attempt to hijack its alien cargo.

Hailing from James S.A. Corey's first book in "The Expanse Series", the Scopuli was found moored to an asteroid by James Holden and his Canterbury crew. The amber-brown mess discovered inside the rigged ship is not to be trifled with, let alone inhaled, eaten, or touched.

Come to think of it, it’s probably much wiser to get out while you can and move along!

Anything that looks like an organic hammer-headed horseshoe lying canted in a rocky ravine on a hostile, uncharted planetoid is best to avoid. Especially when its repeating SOS beacon is translated into its true message… a dire warning to keep curious rubberneckers the hell away!

Once its strange, sexually suggestive openings are penetrated by Nostromo crew members, seeing fossilized giants and oceans of squishy egg pods in the cargo hold would make most reasonable people flee in terror.

We're better off leaving this sleeping nightmare in its resting place.

One of the inspirations for Ridley Scott's "Alien", this Golden Age goodie brings us aboard the sleek silver rescue rocketship, Challenge 142, and locks us inside after a bloodthirsty reptilian alien from Mars decides to catch a lift back to Earth with its new astronaut friends in the far-flung future of... 1973!

Mute, clawed monsters with insatiable appetites for human flesh are never good travel companions in the confines of a steel spacecraft. A wiser choice would have been to have stayed on Mars and used the Challenge 142 as a stylized red planet potato farm.

Need a glowing golden suntan? This vessel was launched from Earth to detonate a nuclear payload within the sun's fury to keep its fusion furnace burning and was never heard from again.

A sister rescue vessel, the Icarus 2, was dispatched as a last resort and encountered this long-abandoned ship drifting near the scorching star. Inside the Icarus 1, its over-tanned Captain Pinback has been caught in an addictive ritual of basking in the sun's brilliant embrace and has gone quite insane.

Back out quietly and toss him a nice bottle of aloe vera lotion.

Lawrence Fishburne's Captain Miller thinks this place is a tomb! Well, that's not a very polite way to describe what I think is one of the most ominous spaceships ever seen on screen.

The fact that this foreboding vessel, designed after the cathedral of Notre Dame, has appeared in Neptune's orbit following its disappearance after entering a black hole should be enough to keep the crew of the Lewis and Clark from steering anywhere close. Nothing good can be happening on that doomed craft considering the seven-year absence.

One second after discovering that the craft punctured a route straight to Hades and returned with some extra baggage, I'd be running for the exit hatch! The welcome mat is out, but there's no need to knock on this airlock.

Basically an "Alien" ripoff, this low-budget cult sci-fi flick has its following, but only from those midnight runs to the video store in the '80s to grab the tape with the craziest-looking alien on the cover.

The Shenandoah is a prospecting explorer sent by a ruthless corporation to claim an alien archaeological site on Saturn's moon, Titan. Assorted chaos ensues when a rival West German spaceship is discovered at the dig site, only for our protagonists to find the crew slaughtered.

The carnivorous monster that creeps onto the Shenandoah suffers from little monster syndrome, but its bite is impressive. Best to have never touched the metallic pods in the subterranean cave and just skipped this homicidal mission entirely.

Jeff Spry is an award-winning screenwriter and veteran freelance journalist covering TV, movies, video games, books, and comics. His work has appeared at SYFY Wire, Inverse, Collider, Bleeding Cool and elsewhere. Jeff lives in beautiful Bend, Oregon amid the ponderosa pines, classic muscle cars, a crypt of collector horror comics, and two loyal English Setters.

Founder and CEO Tiina Lokk takes THR through the humble beginnings of the Estonian fest, its growth, where the Black Nights, black carpet and wolf brands came from, and why even she had doubts at first.

What a difference three decades make! Estonia’s Tallinn Black Nights Film Festival (PÖFF) is celebrating the opening of its 30th edition on Friday, which will screen 230 feature and 259 short films from 87 countries. Its inaugural edition in 1997 had shown a much more modest number of movies – 24 titles from Nordic countries, Germany and France.

Back then, the number of cinemas in Estonia, which had declared its independence in 1991 amid the collapse of the USSR, was still minuscule. And festival film admissions totaled around 6,000, which was seen as a success. Last year, in contrast, PÖFF admissions hit nearly 95,000. Related Stories Movies Milcho Manchevski's 'Sister Brother Manhole Cover' Wins Top Prize at Tokyo Film Fest Movies AFM: Dark Sky Takes 'American Dollhouse' for U.S. (Exclusive)

All this growth has made Tallinn a fixture on the festival circuit for more and more industry folks, and it has elevated it to Northern Europe’s largest film festival. In 2014, also boosted its reputation further by earning FIAPF A-list accreditation, putting it into the company of such venerable fests as Cannes, Venice, Berlin, Sundance, Toronto, Karlovy Vary and Locarno.

PÖFF founder and CEO Tiina Lokk has been the visionary and driving force behind the festival’s arrival in the top tier. Earlier this year, she shifted her focus to overall strategic and developmental direction, giving up her role as festival director, with her daughter Triin Tramberg being promoted to the role of artistic director.

Given its standing today, you may be surprised to hear that Lokk’s idea to launch a film festival in Tallinn wasn’t seen as a slam dunk. And that included her own skepticism. “I had deep doubts,” she tells THR. “Even though I wanted to create the festival because I am a film critic, theorist and historian, and the biggest dream of every film critic is to put together a festival where you can pick your favorite films.”

But Estonia didn’t have a film festival tradition, given that the Soviet Union had only the Moscow Film Festival, which wasn’t even taking place every year. “We had a kind of rolling festival, the All-Union Film Festival, for all 15 republics of the Soviet Union,” she recalls. “Every year it took place in the capital of a different republic. And in my lifetime, I saw only one festival in Tallinn [in 1982], and Estonia was the final republic to host it.”

No surprise then that, as Look puts it, “I wasn’t sure that Estonia was ready to have a regular festival and that it was needed.” After all, the country is quite small, with a population of 1.3 million today.

Also, the post-Soviet years brought a focus on all sorts of challenges and reforms, “but for cinema, it wasn’t a very hopeful time,” she shares. “Nobody knew what to do with cinema, and there wasn’t even money for it in the Ministry of Culture budget. There was even one year when there were zero feature films made.”

The infrastructure for cineasts was minimal. “In the middle of the ’90s, we had three or four cinemas for all of Estonia, and these cinemas were showing only Hollywood blockbusters and Chinese B-grade kung-fu films,” Lokk recalls.

At the same time, foreign film shoots came into Estonia and other parts of the former Soviet Union, driven by an interest in locations that hadn’t been used before and the affordability.

Lokk fell on deaf ears with many politicians with her pitch for a festival or an improved screen infrastructure in Tallinn. “We don’t need that in Estonia,” she recalls a typical response. “If you want to go to cinemas, go to Helsinki or go to Paris. And when I tried to tell them that the cinema world is actually much bigger and much more colorful than only Hollywood and China, they said: ‘Who cares?’ And since it was clear we couldn’t compete with Hollywood, there was a big question mark about whether we needed a national cinema at all. The few Estonian features that were made then were always compared with Hollywood films, which is ridiculous.”

Lokk ran her own distribution company, FilmaMAX, back then and had built an international network that ended up encouraging her to follow her festival dream. “The embassies in Estonia with whom I worked supported me and pushed me to start it,” she tells THR.

She started looking for a hotel venue, only to face rejection after rejection. “Finally, my last option agreed [to do it] and be a sponsor, so we started the festival.”

Money was scarce, with the fest getting some financial support from the diplomatic corps and a “very, very small” amount from the state, Lokk emphasizes. “My friends and classmates also gave us some money.”

In the early days of the Tallinn festival, attendees may not have only had their eyes on film screening schedules, panel discussions and social events, like today, but also on things that these days seem reserved for on-screen action. “In the middle of the ’90s, there were bombs blowing up cars in the street,” Lokk recalls. “The mafia was around. It was a different time.”

In the beginning, the festival took place in early December. “On the festival calendar, that was an absolutely empty place,” Lokk recalls. But soon, the fest moved to November. But no, it was not because of the weather. “November is actually the most hated time in Estonia,” the fest founder tells THR. “It is 0 degrees, and all my life, my dream used to be not to have to be in Tallinn in November. But because November is dark, my experience with distribution was that it was the best-selling time for cinemas.”

Tallinn has, of course, made this a key point in its branding as well. The festival’s English-language name includes those Black Nights, and so does its Estonian acronym PÖFF, which stands for Pimedate Ööde filmifestival, which translates as Black Nights Film Festival.

The festival is also known for swapping the traditional red carpet for its signature black carpet. That tradition dates back to 2016 and symbolizes the dark nights of November in Estonia. But it also comes with a touch of self-irony, as organizers like to mention with a wink, saying the festival lacks both the financial resources and technical requirements for the glamour of a traditional red carpet.

And don’t expect PÖFF to ever go for a super-competitive summer slot on the festival circuit. “If we [scheduled] the festival, let’s say, in May or June and had a White Nights festival, nobody would be going to the cinemas,” Lokk explains. “Box office is playing quite a big role in our budget. And we are still not very popular with politicians and are struggling to get money [from them].”

Not that she is crying wolf. Which brings us to a final key element of the PÖFF brand – its symbol and mascot, said wolf. “All the great festivals have local animals, but most were picked already,” Lokk recalls. “The bear belonged to Berlin. The Lion is Venice’s. So okay, the wolf had not been picked. And the wolf is actually a legendary animal in all our fairy tales and even epics.”

Asked about the wolf’s character, the festival CEO highlights: “It is an ego player but at the same time a big team player. There is very strict organization in wolf society, and so we looked up all the legends about wolves. I saw a documentary about them, Mother Wolf, and one of the last shots in this documentary was when a lonely mother wolf was howling under the full moon. So, I said it has to be our local animal.”

The festival can indeed count on what is dubbed the “Wolf Pack,” a PÖFF community connecting film enthusiasts, culture supporters, companies, guests, as well as volunteers and interns who all contribute time, money, or both to make the festival a success every year.

Speaking of successes. The inaugural Tallinn fest’s opening film came from a big name. It was Drifting Clouds from Finnish auteur Aki Kaurismäki, who was honored with the PÖFF Lifetime Achievement Award in 2006. The film will screen again this year as part of the festival’s 30th anniversary celebration. And the fest once again has attracted such stars as Tim Blake Nelson and Goldshifteh Farahani and their films.

Lokk is proud that the festival has supported the Estonian, and the broader Baltic, film industry, and vice versa, with films from the region now regularly traveling to big festivals around the globe and winning awards. Since 2008, PÖFF has showcased projects from the region in its Baltic Film Competition. Last year, it also launched a Baltic documentary competition.

It has pushed into other areas as well. The festival’s kids and youth-focused Just Film program debuted its Industry Days in 2023, the Industry@Tallinn & Baltic event industry strand has continuously broadened and deepened its offerings, and PÖFF has been strengthening its educational initiatives, Lokk highlights.

Helping celebrate its three decades this year will be three Tallinn exhibitions. “Stars in the Night” pays tribute to PÖFF’s guests through 20 portraits spanning the festival’s history, while “30 PÖFFs. 30 Posters. 30 Stories” showcases all of the festival’s posters for the first time, “telling a story of growth, creativity and the courage to stand out,” organizers say. Finally, “30 PÖFFs, 30 Years of Stories, Thousands of Films and a Million Memories” is designed to “capture the festival’s atmosphere” through moments that have shaped its history.

Given all this history and expansion into new areas over the years, this seemed like a good time to reduce her workload and let others step up, Lokk says. “The festival has become big, I am getting older, and there is a new generation,” she tells THR. “It is very important that the head of programming is feeling the pulse of the audience.”

So, what lies ahead for the Tallinn festival will partly depend on any changes that Tramberg may pursue. For now, she wants to keep a close eye on “what works and what doesn’t.” She also tells THR: “Of course, I have ideas about what the festival can become and where the roof is, but the main goal is that the festival stays relevant and that, in today’s society, people continue to come to a festival and to the cinemas. This is a moment to explore emotions together.”

And while the duo may not have any immediate big changes to share, Lokk signals that she continues, as she has done throughout the history of PÖFF, to look for future opportunities. “We have our 30th edition this year,” she says. “Now there are the next 10 years where we have to think about what direction we are taking.”

From a close encounter between Mars and Jupiter to dazzling Venus and elusive Mercury, November offers plenty of planetary highlights. Here's when and where to look.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

This is a great month for planet watching, either in the evenings or mornings. During convenient evening hours, the planet of choice is Saturn, visible well up in the southern sky during mid-to-late evening hours. Telescopically, the southern side of its famous ring system is currently tilted about 6½ degrees to our line of sight.

Around the middle of the night, Mars and Jupiter come into view above the east-northeast horizon and just before the break of dawn are in excellent position, soaring high in the southern sky in the vicinity of the Sickle of Leo the Lion. Watch how Mars approaches Jupiter early in the month, passes it on Nov. 16, then spends the rest of the month sailing away to the east. Meanwhile, in the predawn morning sky, Venus literally vaults into prominence as the month progresses. And from midmonth on through the end of November, Mercury asserts itself, appearing as a very bright "star" to the far lower left of Venus.

In our schedule, remember that when measuring the angular separation between two celestial objects, your clenched fist held at arm's length measures roughly 10 degrees. Here, we present a schedule below which provides some of the best planet viewing times as well directing you as to where to look to see them

Reminder: On Nov. 1 — where applicable — change clocks back one hour from Daylight Saving Time. On this date, the clock hour from 1 to 2:00 a.m. is repeated, thus making this day the longest of the year: 25 hours long. The mnemonic is: "Spring Ahead, Fall Back."

Mercury, hidden during inferior conjunction with the sun on Nov. 4, will emerge in the eastern morning sky after the second week of the month to undergo an excellent morning apparition for the Northern Hemisphere. This rocky little world arrives at its greatest western elongation (20 degrees) from the sun on Nov. 20; its most favorable morning apparition of the year for mid-northern observers. From Nov. 16 to Nov. 26 speedy Mercury will rise in the east-southeast before the beginning of astronomical twilight, more than 95 minutes before sunrise.

Venus is a good reason to be up at the crack of dawn in November; it's a silvery lamp that rises above the east-southeast horizon. Venus was at inferior conjunction on Oct. 24. But the steep angle of the ecliptic at dawn in late autumn helps Venus vault noticeably higher with each passing day for observers at mid-northern latitudes. On Nov. 1, it rises 55 minutes before the sun. But just several days later on Nov. 5, viewers around 40 degrees north latitude can see Venus come up one hour and 25 minutes before the sun and shine 15 degrees above the horizon at sunrise. As November ends, Venus rises nearly 3½ hours before the sun and hangs nearly 35 degrees up at sunrise.

All month Venus brightens impressively and on the penultimate day of the month it will reach the pinnacle of its magnificent brightness, shining at magnitude -4.9, rising almost 3½ hours before the sun. If there's snow on the ground, check for shadows made by Venus's light. Through a telescope, the phase of the planet looks most remarkable early in the month. That's when you may be able to glimpse Venus when it's only a few percent illuminated, a hairline crescent close to an arcminute long; about 1/30 the apparent diameter of the moon. Venus is not alone in the dawn sky.

Its leap takes it up into the proximity of the bluish 1st-magnitude star Spica in Virgo on the morning of Nov. 3. The star will be sitting 2.4 degrees to the upper right of Venus. During this month, Venus seems to perform a dos-à-dos with Spica and at first seems destined to soar up and catch it. Instead, the closest it gets to this star is 1.8 degrees to its upper left early on the morning of Nov. 19.

On the morning of Nov. 7, a striking array of a waning crescent moon, brilliant Venus and Spica awaits early risers low in the east-southeast sky about an hour before sunrise. The trio will be bunched together inside of a circle measuring only about 2½ degrees in diameter.

Mars, shining at magnitude +0.9, is in Leo in the morning sky and is easily found on the morning of Nov. 2, using the moon as a guide. That day it sits a couple of degrees to the left of the moon. In addition, on that date, Mars is positioned 5 degrees to the upper right of much brighter Jupiter.

Mars has been hiding in the glare of the sun, or in the dead of the early morning hours, for the last year and a quarter. Now it finally rises in the east before midnight. Each night, watch the orange-yellow planet move a little closer to Jupiter. They'll be in conjunction on Nov. 16 (See Jupiter below).

On the morning of Nov. 26, Mars, having brightened to magnitude +0.6, passes 1.7 degrees to the upper left of the first magnitude star Regulus in Leo. The color contrast between the orange-yellow planet and blue-white star is striking, especially in binoculars.

Jupiter is high enough for a steady telescopic view by 3 a.m. But its dusky cloud belts and Red Spot can be seen more clearly when the planet is highest in the southeast soon after dawn breaks.

On Nov. 3, shortly after 1 a.m. local time, look low toward the east-northeast horizon to watch the moon slowly ascend the sky. The 1st magnitude star Regulus will be evident sitting a degree to the moon's left. And sitting about 5 degrees above the moon will be Jupiter, appearing as a brilliant "star" shining with a steady, silvery light.

Mars passes 1.2 degrees to the upper left of Jupiter on Nov. 16; the giant planet outshining the red planet 13-fold. Late on Nov. 29 and into the early hours of Nov. 30, look low toward the east-northeast horizon for a gathering of the waning gibbous moon, with Jupiter, Regulus and Mars. These four celestial bodies cover an expanse of roughly 7 degrees going from right to left. Best views will come around the time of the break of dawn when they'll appear to soar high in the southern sky.

Saturn is situated in the northeast corner of the non-zodiacal constellation of Cetus the Whale (or Sea Monster). It crosses the southern meridian around 9:45 p.m. at the beginning of November and about two hours earlier at the month's end. All evening, it is excellently placed for telescopic viewing of its glorious ball and rings. At magnitude +0.6, Saturn is easily the brightest point of light in its section of the heavens. It can also be told from the stars by its steady, yellowish light.

On the evening of Nov. 18, take note of Saturn mimicking a bright "star" shining about 6 degrees below the waxing gibbous moon.

Joe Rao serves as an instructor and guest lecturer at New York's Hayden Planetarium. He writes about astronomy for Natural History magazine, Sky and Telescope, The Old Farmer's Almanac and other publications.

Joe Rao is Space.com's skywatching columnist, as well as a veteran meteorologist and eclipse chaser who also serves as an instructor and guest lecturer at New York's Hayden Planetarium. He writes about astronomy for Natural History magazine, Sky & Telescope and other publications. Joe is an 8-time Emmy-nominated meteorologist who served the Putnam Valley region of New York for over 21 years. You can find him on Twitter and YouTube tracking lunar and solar eclipses, meteor showers and more. To find out Joe's latest project, visit him on Twitter.

#712. Hollywood Quietly Banning Prediction Market Betting on Movie News, Release Dates (Exclusive)

Employees at studios and production companies are being warned against profiting off their knowledge of insider information. But experts say there's almost no way to stop it.

If you’re an industry insider tempted to drop a few thousand on Kalshi predicting who will be cast as the next James Bond, think again.

The Hollywood Reporter has learned studios and production companies have been quietly issuing new guidelines to employees warning them not to engage in prediction market betting.

The warnings prohibit employees from placing bets on news events like studio earnings, casting, or even release dates. Passing information along to friends and family for them to place bets is likewise forbidden. At least one company set up a hotline where staffers can anonymously report on their fellow employees suspected of placing bets. Related Stories Business Kalshi Accuses Netflix of Defamation Over Trailer for Prediction Markets Documentary News Inside the $5 Million Betting Frenzy Over Taylor Swift's Wedding

In a way, such updates are an expansion on longstanding rules which forbid employees from insider trading in the stock market. And many instances of prediction market profiteering using insider corporate information might violate federal law already. But with prediction markets allowing betting on everything from who will be cast as the next Wonder Woman to who will be eliminated on Dancing with the Stars, the opportunities for stealthily cashing in on insider knowledge has dramatically increased.

“You now have, essentially, an explosion in the number of employers who have to think about insider trading rules from an ethical standpoint,” says Joshua Mitts, a law professor at Columbia University who has extensively studied the legalities and trends surrounding prediction market betting. “And totally apart from the question of criminal prosecution, is just the compliance problem — educating your employees on what’s allowed.”

THR’s parent company, PMC, which also owns Dick Clark Productions and other publications such as Variety and Deadline, has likewise updated its employee handbook to ban prediction market betting in recent weeks. Among other things, the company forbids betting on “award nominations, casting decisions, production timelines and release dates.”

Some improper betting among entertainment industry insiders has already made headlines, yet the reported cases almost certainly represent just the tip of the iceberg in terms of betting behind the scenes.

In February, Kalshi disclosed that a video editor working for MrBeast’s company made $5,000 by improperly using confidential information to place bets about MrBeast content. The employee was fired and slapped with a $20,000 penalty.

While in April, a Puck column revealed someone who worked on a CBS competition show and had been making money through prediction markets.

One TV network source lamented that even though their company’s insider trading policy prohibits betting on prediction markets related to their work, the opportunity for insider bets remain rampant. For example, there are markets on what a guest will say on the Tonight Show, Saturday Night Live or other talk shows, many of which are pretaped or have dress rehearsals. Some of those shows have audiences made up of the public, and those people could bet without fear of breaking any rules.

Interestingly, one major betting site, BetOnline, temporarily pulled its page allowing people to wager on the who will be cast as the next James Bond this week after the final auditions were expected to have taken place. The reason, according to a representative: “Sharp money” suddenly came down hard in favor of Callum Turner, surging him to the top of the odds chart above longtime favorite Jack Lowden, causing internal concern that the bets might be the result of a credible leak.

In March, a study by Mitts and University of Haifa’s Moran Ofir estimated $143 million in anomalous profit being made across Polymarket during a two-year period, a figure that’s certainly ramped up dramatically since given the number of betting categories that have increased.

While some prediction market betting has been argued to have societal value — for instance, a company hedging against a costly change in government policy — Mitts notes betting on entertainment industry news isn’t really one of them.

“There’s a high degree of asymmetric information [in terms of a handful of studio insiders knowing certain upcoming announcements], and a high degree of secret information, but there’s very little social utility to having this priced correctly,” says Mitts. “With a straight face, can you really say society is making better decisions because we know the probability of who’s going to win a reality TV show, or the probability of a movie sequel?”

That said, while a couple of insiders have been caught betting on entertainment news, studios will have a very tough time stopping employees from betting. Prediction market bets can be difficult for employers to trace to individual employees, particularly on blockchain-based platforms. “With blockchain-based trading, it can be basically impossible [to catch a better] if you know how to use a mixer correctly and know how to hide your identity behind multiple layers of intermediation,” Mitts says. “So it’s quite hard for employers to suss it out through an open source investigation.”

Perhaps most famously (and worrisomely), in February six newly created Polymarket wallets earned $1.2 million by accurately betting on U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. Nobody has been caught.

Over the summer the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which regulates prediction markets in the U.S., put out an open call for the industry to weigh in on what should be legal to trade on, and what shouldn’t. The CFTC declared that betting on award shows like the Oscars and Emmys should be allowed “because the award turns on evaluative judgments, not on measurable occurrences dependent on the participants’ skill or athletic ability in the activity itself, it is a contest, not gaming.”However, it was less certain about other forms of entertainment:“For example, should game shows, reality show competitions, pageants and similar events be considered to be ’gaming’?” the CFTC wrote. “The Commission notes that game shows are typically subject to varying standards intended to promote impartiality and fair competition. Other competitions may allow departure from such standards to enhance their entertainment value. Music and talent competitions often have similarities to elections. How, if at all, should the Commission consider these characteristics in the context of event contracts involving these activities?”A number of comments to the CFTC complained about bets made on the last season of Survivor, where the winner appears to have been tagged early, thanks to aggressive bets on prediction markets.

In a quirk of financial history, there are only two types of prediction market bets explicitly outlawed by Congress in the Onion Futures Act of 1958: Onion futures contract, and motion picture box office receipts. In other words, it is illegal to offer bets on how much revenue a film will see at the box office, despite all the myriad other bets available that touch on the entertainment business.

If regulators decide to crack down on prediction market betting, Mitts notes that the entertainment industry might be a prime candidate for increased regulatory scrutiny given the high potential for insider trading and “low social benefit” of the bets. “If you’re going to prioritize an investigation or strict policies, it would seem that these kinds of entertainment markets might be good candidates for that.”

#711. NASA's Swift space telescope is about to crash to Earth. Where will it fall?

Swift is expected to crash back to Earth in the next few days.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Update for 2:45 p.m. ET on Nov. 4: NASA's Swift space telescope fell to Earth today at 7:39 a.m. EST (1239 GMT) over Indonesia. Read our story here.

NASA's Swift space telescope is expected to crash back to Earth in the next few days.

The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory will reenter Earth's atmosphere in an uncontrolled fashion, after a robotic rescue mission failed to boost the scope to a higher orbit.

Swift launched to Earth orbit back in November 2004. Over the next two decades, it studied gamma-ray bursts — the most powerful explosions in the universe — and other cosmic objects and events using a trio of telescopes: a Burst Alert Telescope (BAT), an X-Ray Telescope (XRT), and its Ultraviolet/Optical Telescope (UVOT).

On Oct. 20, NASA reported that Swift's orbit had decayed to 171 miles (275 kilometers) above Earth and that the roughly 3,300-pound (1,500-kilogram) observatory was no longer able to compensate for the effects of the increased drag. It entered safe mode, followed by Swift's operations team at Pennsylvania State University sending a command to the spacecraft that effectively ended its operations ahead of its destructive and fiery nose-dive.

It's unclear at the moment exactly when and where Swift will plunge to Earth. But researchers definitely have their eyes peeled.

In physics fashion, for the most part, what goes up must come down — with more space hardware to follow.

Thanks to the growing surge in low Earth orbit constellations and technology refresh cycles, there are 10 times more objects reentering per year than there were just five years ago, said Darren McKnight, a senior technical fellow at LeoLabs, a company that keeps a watchful eye on what's going on above our planet.

"It is unfortunate that Swift was not 'reorbited,' but from a reentry hazard perspective it is a small portion of the stuff coming back in. The rub on this, of course, is that, while many people bemoan the reentry of more objects, I am much more upset about the rapid rate of abandoning massive objects above 400 miles [644 km]," McKnight told Space.com.

Swift will likely disintegrate sufficiently upon reentry to not pose a ground casualty hazard, McKnight said. However, the internal workings of the observatory's X-ray and optical telescope might survive, McKnight said.

Similar in view is Dean Sladen, a quality manager and aerospace engineer at the U.K. precision-components supplier Accu Components.

"Once Swift falls to about 120 kilometers [75 miles], the end usually comes within a few minutes. The air in front of it heats up so much that the satellite will start to glow. Solar panels and antennas are typically the first to tear off, and at around 78 kilometers [48 miles], roughly eight times the height of a passing airliner, the main body breaks apart. Most of it will melt and vaporize," said Sladen.

While it isn't yet known exactly where any surviving pieces will land, Sladen noted that Swift's orbit only passes over a band within about 21 degrees of the equator.

"That band is mostly ocean, though it also crosses populated parts of Africa, South and Southeast Asia and Latin America," he said.

As for which parts are most likely to survive and reach ocean or ground, Sladen pointed out that most of Swift's body is aluminum, wiring and electronics, which melt away early in the reentry process. What reaches Earth is usually small, dense and heat-resistant, such as titanium, steel and glass.

"The most likely survivors are its six heavy reaction wheels, the spinning flywheels it used to aim itself, along with tougher telescope parts such as lenses and mirrors. Its mask of around 52,000 tiny lead tiles will almost certainly melt. Only a handful of small, scorched fragments are expected to make it down — nothing recognizable as a telescope," Sladen said.

Sladen said that, at the current time, it appears that no detailed risk assessment has been published for Swift's fall.

"However, this does not mean NASA has not done the work," said Sladen.

"NASA's own orbital debris requirements state that the risk of human casualty from surviving debris shall not exceed one in 10,000, so it is highly likely this work has been completed but not published," he told Space.com. "Personally, I believe it should be published, as NASA has done with previous satellites. The risk is almost certainly very small, but it would give people a clear, factual picture rather than guesswork."

Sladen added that there's far more focus on how a satellite's life ends these days than there was in the past.

"Many now carry enough propulsion to steer themselves into a remote stretch of ocean, or are built from materials designed to burn up completely, an approach called 'design for demise.' NASA and the European Space Agency limit the chance of anyone being hurt by a reentry to one in 10,000, and if a satellite can't meet that, it's expected to come down in a controlled way," said Sladen.

So, should people be worried about having a nasty run-in with Swift leftovers?

Sladen doesn't think so. NASA has said that harm to anyone on the ground is unlikely, and LeoLabs also describes the risk as very small. Most of the spacecraft will burn up, and any surviving pieces will most likely fall into the sea, he said.

"The real concern is the long-term trend. With more satellites being launched than ever, the number of uncontrolled reentries is growing, which is why designing satellites to come down safely matters more and more," Sladen concluded.

Leonard David is an award-winning space journalist who has been reporting on space activities for more than 50 years. Currently writing as Space.com's Space Insider Columnist among his other projects, Leonard has authored numerous books on space exploration, Mars missions and more, with his latest being "Moon Rush: The New Space Race" published in 2019 by National Geographic. He also wrote "Mars: Our Future on the Red Planet" released in 2016 by National Geographic. Leonard  has served as a correspondent for SpaceNews, Scientific American and Aerospace America for the AIAA. He has received many awards, including the first Ordway Award for Sustained Excellence in Spaceflight History in 2015 at the AAS Wernher von Braun Memorial Symposium. You can find out Leonard's latest project at his website and on Twitter.
